items.title: To save Esan language from extinction, I’ll do anything – Dr. Mabel Imooje
items.description: By Fred Iwenjora Dr. Mabel Imooje holds a doctorate degree in linguistics from Bayero University, Kano. The staff of National Institute for Hospitality and Tourism, Kano is making name as an advocate for the survival of Esan Language seen by many researches as one of the indigenous languages set to go extinct if drastic measures are not taken. Imooje travels across Nigeria at her spare time meeting Esan speaking people, giving them reasons to strive to sustain the language. The associate member of Nigerian Institute of Translators and Interpreters. (NITI) tells FRED IWENJORA the inspiration behind this arduous advocacy. She also discusses the hurdles as well as triumphs so far. “My inspiration comes from my passion for Esan language. The language is so very hard wired in my brain that no one needs ask where I come from whenever I speak. Any Nigerian or Edo state native does not need to ask of my tribe before he/she with affirmation will say, ‘you are an Esan’. “My accent is so strong in my speech, and I feel it’s impact should be used in improving language instruction, develop teaching materials and create learning resources for our dear language. Have you documented these in a book? Not yet but it is in the pipeline. I have been fascinated by languages and always wished to speak about theories and workings of indigenous languages. What course of study prepared you for this? I first started with an NCE in English/Social Studies. Later, I got a degree and a master’s in English before switching to linguistics at doctorate level. I did this to really understand how indigenous languages work and of course with special interest in Esan language. I will also say here that I love my language and wanted it documented from my own point of view. On why she went local rather than beginning from abroad with French, Spanish, Italian or even Mandarin, she hinted that “Going local is to encourage indigenous languages to pop up amongst the foreign languages that you just mentioned. No one watches his or her inheritance erode through wreckless abandonments. I decided to go local to save my language from extinction. Esan is both a people and a language spoken in five local government areas in the Edo Central Senatorial district. It is one of the endangered languages of the world. It should be noted that several factors cause language endangerment. These include diminishing number of the native speakers, age, failure to use the language by the children, negative attitude of the native speaker towards the language, rural – urban shift and so on, just to mention but a few. Therefore, my going local is to lend my voice to other crusaders to say ‘no’ to extinction of indigenous languages. You mean we shouldn’t chase foreign languages? I did not mean that. Proficiency in English and any other foreign languages is good for socio-economic mobility and national integration but it can also lead to marginalisation of indigenous languages. The priority given to foreign languages, English precisely in Nigeria, is gradually making the already endangered languages non relevant. And I am saying no. Speak the language, save the language I dare say. I feel that their view may be a wrong perspective because I see myself creating an ideal position by embracing the value of indigenous language while still contributing to broader linguistic cultural and professional communities. I also see it as an ample opportunity to provide expertise and contributions, foster community and trust, promote linguistic and cultural diversity and inform global initiatives with local perspectives. There must be hurdles presenting itself as you do these? Of course, yes! It is a very big tasking job that has a lot of challenges. It costs a lot of money to travel from one state to another to sensitive the native speakers on the need to speak their indigenous language, and save the language for the sake of posterity. The native speakers need to have something to pass on to the next generation as they also inherited it. Language is a cultural heritage that should be cherished. Many shy away from speaking their indigenous language because they think it’s a kind of status thing to speak foreign languages. But this is mere ignorance! I have not got sponsors. None yet. Another challenge in this task is getting to meet the chief custodians of the culture which are the kings and traditional rulers. I have faced a lot of disappointments. Like the biblical saying goes: “No one puts his hands on the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom”. Therefore, I have to keep moving. But I wont deny that I still get support of praises and encouragements though not in cash and I am happy about that for now. Any triumphs? Of course, yes. I have recorded triumphs. I feel elated each time I watch the videos of the meetings that I have had especially with the King of Ekpoma and leaders of his kingdom. I spoke out for the sustenance of Esan language. I told them that we inherited the language that we speak today. Therefore we need to keep speaking it so that we can also pass it to the next generation. “I told my King ,that posterity will not forgive us if we cannot sustain the language which gives us identity wherever we find ourselves. I told him to encourage the people to speak the language and save the language. I also told King of Ekpoma that Esan should be spoken in every home in Esanland as against the use of English. The king told the chiefs to take the message to every home. I wish to add that I am not only concerned about Esan language but all indigenous languages in Nigeria. It’s a project: Speak the language, save the language. As far as I am privileged, this initiative will extend to other tribes whose languages are also endangered and going extinct. I have only started from mine, Esan. Vanguard News The post To save Esan language from extinction, I’ll do anything – Dr. Mabel Imooje appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Emilia Redolar, neurocientífica: “Como mujer trans, no me siento tan laboralmente empoderada como cuando me llamaba Diego”
items.description: Un recuerdo infantil de la doctora Emilia Redolar (Teruel, 52 años) tiene como escenario la carpintería de su abuelo, un cuchillo y el deseo de cortarse el pene. Su abuela le enseñó a coser, pero, al descubrir que se había hecho una falda, le pidió que eso quedase entre ellas. Al iniciar los trámites de su cambio de sexo en el DNI, Redolar eligió llamarse como ella: Emilia (dejando atrás el nombre de Diego, con el que había firmado sus anteriores libros ). Hoy, tras cinco décadas sintiéndose mujer en cuerpo de hombre , firma su primer libro con ese nombre. La entrevista es en el piso de Sant Cugat (Barcelona) que comparte con su hija Martina. items.title: Radiografía del sistema de seguridad que dejó de funcionar antes del accidente de Urda: casi una caída cada dos días
items.description: A las 8.31 del miércoles , seis trenes que circulan por la línea de alta velocidad que une Madrid-Sevilla y se reparten por un tramo de 63 kilómetros se ven afectados por el mismo problema: se ha caído el sistema LZB, que sirve para que dos convoyes no coincidan en el mismo cantón o pequeño segmento de la línea. La consecuencia es inmediata. Todos se paran. Saben que van a tener que operar al amparo los sistemas ASFA (que mide la distancia entre trenes por balizas y es capaz de detenerlos si superan ciertas barreras de seguridad) y BSL (que se comunica con los trenes por señales en los laterales de la vía). Los maquinistas se ponen en contacto con el centro de coordinación de Adif en Atocha (Madrid), donde nadie parece sorprendido por la situación, según los audios publicados por EL PAÍS . En lo que va de año, el LZB ha dejado de estar en servicio en 170 ocasiones, según explica luego el ministro Óscar Puente. Eso supone que está desactivado casi una vez cada dos días, con incidencias de diferente duración. En este caso, la reactivación de la marcha, para la que se aplican protocolos incorrectos , lleva al desastre: un AVE lanzado a entre 160 y 200 kilómetros por hora percute contra un Iryo totalmente parado en Urda (Toledo), provocando al menos 69 muertos y centenares de heridos de diversa consideración. Seguir leyendo

items.title: 69 autopsias en tres días: la carrera forense para identificar a las víctimas
items.description: Son las diez de la mañana de este viernes en la casa de ejercicios El Buen Pastor, en Toledo, cuando la Guardia Civil entra y reúne a los familiares en el jardín. Han pasado 72 horas desde el accidente ferroviario y los agentes les transmiten un mensaje: tienen que prepararse para el peor de los escenarios. Un grito de dolor rompe el silencio que sigue a esas palabras. Una mujer cae de rodillas al suelo mientras quienes la acompañan tratan de sujetarla. El hilo de esperanza al que todavía se aferraban las familias empieza a deshacerse. Después de esa visita, nada vuelve a ser igual en la casa. Entre las más de cien personas congregadas allí se abre entonces un debate doloroso, si empezar a comunicar las malas noticias al resto de la familia o esperar un poco más. “A veces es mejor la hostia directamente que sostenida en el tiempo”, le dice una mujer a su madre. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El arzobispo de Toledo sobre los desaparecidos del accidente de tren: “La esperanza no quita nada del dolor”
items.description: Todo el dolor del mundo cabe en el jardín arbolado que se extiende ante la casa sacerdotal Buen Pastor de Toledo , el lugar habilitado en la capital castellanomanchega para acoger a decenas de familiares de las víctimas desaparecidas. Aquí comen, algunos duermen y esperan noticias desde hace dos días. La gente charla en corrillos diseminados, en un ambiente en el que se mezclan la tristeza, la frustración, la rabia y la incertidumbre; las personas se abrazan de esa forma larga en la que a uno le da tiempo a acariciar la espalda del otro, se oyen durísimas conversaciones en voz baja —“Ella es pequeña, pero madura…”; “es bueno que pueda llevar una flor a una lápida”— y de vez en cuando se eleva un llanto desconsolado que provoca un nudo en el estómago. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Una dentellada de desgracia
items.description: En el museo Metropolitano de Nueva York me fijé por primera vez en la cabeza de leona de la diosa Sekmet. Era una exposición sobre los saberes de la medicina en el Antiguo Egipt o. En un vestíbulo en penumbra, que tenía una atmósfera inevitable de templo, relucía la superficie muy pulida del basalto, la diosa sentada en su trono, esculpida a una escala mayor que la humana, con una majestad definitiva, una serenidad amenazante. Sekmet es la diosa de la guerra y la peste, de la desgracia súbita y de la curación. Su aliento de fuego asolaba la vegetación y expandía el desierto. Cuando Ra, asustado por la iniquidad de los seres humanos, decidió exterminarlos, Sekmet avanzaba sobre la tierra extendiendo la mortandad universal como una gran mancha de sangre. El Jehová del Génesis tuvo un arrepentimiento parecido. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los muertos y el ‘show’
items.description: Así que todo esto empezó con una mujer muerta. Se llamaba Maricarmen. La codicia privada y la indiferencia pública acabaron con su vida. Mucha gente se echó a la calle. Se llenaron las plazas. Todos se pusieron graves y convocaron elecciones. Entonces el motivo original comenzó a olvidarse. Y llegó Broncano, y las camisas vaqueras, y las risas, y los culos y los coños que comen unos y otras. Y luego el youtuber Jordi Wild anunció que todos los candidatos habían elegido su canal para venderse ante la ciudadanía. Iba a ser una campaña —después de una persona muerta por un problema que resquebraja a un país entero— de broncanos y YouTube. Para qué el periodismo. Para qué las cosas importantes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿La IA es herramienta o creador?
items.description: En las Metamorfosis de Ovidio la historia de Pigmalión acaba bien. El escultor, célibe, que reprocha a las mujeres que ha conocido sus “numerosos vicios”, esculpe un marfil al que besa, al que viste con gemas, perlas y vestidos. Sabe que se enamora de lo falso. Cuando hace su ofrenda a Venus, no se atreve a pedir que la estatua se convierta en su esposa: pide, con timidez, una “semejante” a la de marfil. La diosa entiende lo que de verdad desea, y cuando Pigmalión vuelve a casa y besa la figura, el marfil se ablanda bajo sus dedos, se entibia, es carne. A fuerza de deseo, la imitación se vuelve verdadera, y deja de importar la diferencia entre una forma “con la que ninguna mujer nacer puede” y una mujer nacida. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Supremo admite a 69 personas y tres asociaciones como afectados por la suspensión del voto a los nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’
items.description: Tres asociaciones y casi 70 particulares figuran ya como afectados en el procedimiento del Tribunal Supremo que ha derivado en la suspensión del voto para los nacionalizados por la ley de nietos. La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo emplazó a personarse el pasado 12 de octubre a los más de 163.000 nuevos españoles a los que ha retirado el derecho al sufragio, y, una vez terminado el plazo de cinco días abierto por el tribunal y examinadas todas las solicitudes, los jueces han aceptado la personación de 69 particulares y de la Asociación de Extranjeristas en Red, el Centro de Descendientes de Españoles Unidos (Cedeu) y la Asociación Pro Derechos Humanos de Andalucía, según la documentación a la que ha tenido acceso este periódico. Para todos ellos ha abierto un nuevo plazo de tres días para que presenten alegaciones sobre el procedimiento. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Y Esperanza Aguirre soltó “una lágrima y todo” por Ignacio González
items.description: Esperanza Aguirre, expresidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, tiene muy clara una cosa: el día que supo que su sucesor al frente del Gobierno, Ignacio González, había entrado en prisión provisional, se le cayó “una lágrima y todo”. Ocurre que su frase, pronunciada el jueves a las puertas del edificio en el que juzgan el caso Lezo , revela lo que no tiene tan claro Aguirre: en qué caso de corrupción acababa de declarar ella como testigo cuando se enteró de la noticia. “Era Gürtel, me parece”, dice dos veces. Su confusión es el reflejo de una época. La antigua baronesa (2003-2012) ha declarado a lo largo de los años en los juzgados que investigan las tramas de corrupción de la Gürtel , la Púnica , la Lezo o el Campus de la Justicia . Nunca ha sido condenada por nada. Pero tanto trasiego judicial nublaría la memoria de cualquiera. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Una decena de países europeos comparten pruebas sobre las torturas de Israel a los integrantes de la flotilla
items.description: Una decena de países europeos sigue el rastro de los abusos cometidos contra sus connacionales mientras participaban en las expediciones de la Global Sumud Flotilla que llevaban ayuda humanitaria a Gaza y fueron interceptadas por Israel en aguas internacionales. Las fiscalías de 10 Estados miembros de la Unión Europea —España, Francia, Italia, Portugal, Bélgica, Países Bajos, Polonia, Eslovaquia, Suecia y Finlandia—, además de Australia, han colaborado y compartido información sobre las causas e investigaciones abiertas tras las denuncias contra políticos, funcionarios y mandos militares israelíes, incluidos ministros del Gabinete de Benjamín Netanyahu, por tortura, secuestro, malos tratos y otros delitos. Así lo han confirmado a EL PAÍS fuentes jurídicas que participaron en la reunión, celebrada el 16 de septiembre en La Haya. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las claves del robo del siglo en Binance: qué ocurrió, quién está detrás y cómo puede sobrevivir la empresa
items.description: Binance, la mayor plataforma cripto del mundo , ha vivido unas 24 horas convulsas. A última hora del jueves, anunció que había sido víctima de un ciberataque, algo cada vez más común en el mundo cripto. Pero con el pasar de las horas quedó claro que no se trataba de un simple incidente, sino del peor ataque cibernético de la historia de los activos digitales. Unos atacantes, probablemente vinculados a Corea del Norte, consiguieron sustraer unos 6.300 millones de dólares en activos de la plataforma, cuatro veces más que los que robaron el año pasado al exchange Bybit. Tras el incidente, la empresa se apresuró a asegurar que cubrirá todas las pérdidas, calmando los nervios de los usuarios y de los inversores. No obstante, los temores crecen en el sector, ya que este incidente demuestra que ninguna plataforma es demasiado grande para ser vulnerable. Seguir leyendo

¿Fallo humano? De verdad, tronco, de verdad
items.description: Escucho a los operarios del centro de control de Atocha en los audios que señalan el error humano de los trabajadores antes de que se diera la orden equivocada. No entiendo todo lo que dicen, hay mucho código, palabras técnicas que no comprendo, hay también ruido, consultas, confusión. Escucho otra vez sin atender al mensaje, solo al tono, a esa otra cualidad del lenguaje que traslada no solo información sino también experiencia y trastienda personal (y laboral). Escucho entonces voces humanas, voces superadas y acostumbradas a su desbordamiento. “De verdad, tronco, de verdad”, protesta el operario del centro de control nada más dictar la instrucción errónea. ¿De qué se queja? Vuelvo a escuchar todos los audios. No escucho ya el error humano, más bien el fallo imperdonable de un sistema negligente. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Dentro del palacio veneciano de Dries Van Noten: “Tiene algo grandioso y tierno al mismo tiempo”
items.description: La inquilina más famosa de todos los palacios venecianos, Peggy Guggenheim, resumió muy bien el hechizo de la ciudad: “Siempre se da por supuesto que Venecia es el lugar ideal para una luna de miel. Es un grave error. Vivir en Venecia, o incluso visitarla, significa enamorarse de la propia ciudad. No queda ya sitio en el corazón para nadie más”. La millonaria neoyorquina se prendó de Venecia de joven, pero cuando cumplió su sueño de mudarse allí, en 1949 –tenía 50 años–, lo hizo con todo el equipo: se instaló en el Palazzo Venier, un singular edificio inacabado al final del Gran Canal (su dueño se arruinó antes de empezar el primer piso), y lo convirtió en el escenario de su independencia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Alba Carrillo, sesión de descontrol: “Rufián me ilusiona mental y sexualmente”
items.description: “Permítame decirle que la tele no le hace justicia”, le dice un camarero. “¿Verdad? En persona soy bastante más lista”, replica rápidamente ella. “Eso no lo sé. Me refería a que es usted más guapa en persona. Muchísimo más guapa”, apunta el empleado del bar, un poco desconcertado por la reacción de su interlocutora. “Ah, gracias. Eso me lo dicen mucho”, reconoce ella con un deje de resignación. Alba Carrillo (Madrid, 40 años) lleva toda su vida lidiando con hombres que solo la quieren ver como “la cara bonita”, “el pibón”, “la tía buena”. Siempre ha sido más que eso. No fue la maniquí dócil de Supermodelo , el reality show con el que debutó hace casi dos décadas. Tampoco fue la novia trofeo del piloto Fonsi Nieto , ni la mujer sumisa y silenciosa del tenista Feliciano López . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Cuando la cocaína destruye más allá del tabique nasal: del paladar a la base del cráneo
items.description: La cocaína no paró tras perforar el tabique nasal de Juan, un joven en la treintena que consumía a diario. Luego taladró su paladar y destruyó parte de los huesos que separan la nariz del cerebro. El líquido cefalorraquídeo, que protege el sistema nervioso central, estaba saliendo por esa oquedad cuando ingresó en la UCI, donde llegó con una grave afección neurológica. Tras retirar los tejidos necrosados, los cirujanos lograron cerrar el agujero, pero el consumo continuó y el paciente acabó falleciendo por una neumonía por aspiración, al llegar a los pulmones sustancias que deberían acabar en el aparato digestivo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El vaivén regulatorio y las elecciones ya impactan el mercado del alquiler de viviendas: se paralizan contratos y cae la oferta
items.description: La sucesión de cambios normativos ha sumido al mercado del alquiler en una incertidumbre inédita. En apenas unas semanas, entre septiembre y octubre, el Congreso tumbó los decretos de vivienda aprobados por el Gobierno y el Ejecutivo respondió con dos nuevas normas, pendientes todavía de convalidación por la Diputación Permanente . A menos de un mes de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre, propietarios e inquilinos desconocen todavía cuál será el marco regulatorio definitivo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Daniel Fuentes, economista y profesor: “Generosidad en las pensiones no significa abundancia”
items.description: El economista y profesor en la Universidad de Alcalá Daniel Fuentes Castro (Ourense, 1975) intenta mediante la evidencia científica y los datos templar la guerra cultural entre generaciones que colea en el debate público. Con su libro Nadie elige cuándo nace (Ed. Shackleton) bucea en la singularidad económica de cada generación para concluir que es necesario un pacto de rentas intergeneracional. Para el autor, las compensaciones pueden ser necesarias pero la prioridad es evitar que se produzca la desigualdad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘24 Hour Party People’, aquella historia real de desmadre por amor a la música y al arte de perder millones
items.description: Hay que agradecer a Michael Winterbottom, director de 24 Hour Party People (2002), que huyera de los clichés que hacen de las películas que retratan tribus musicales hagiografías insufribles. Porque aunque la película estrenada esté titulada por la canción del mismo nombre de Happy Mondays y se venda como la caótica historia de Factory, aquella discográfica británica que marcó la música de los años ochenta con grupos como New Order, el director convierte el filme en la biografía camuflada de uno de sus cuatro fundadores, Tony Wilson. Seguir leyendo Protagonistas secundarios Winterbottom convirtió a los otros tres fundadores de Factory en personajes menores. Una injusticia que sin embargo ayuda a no desviar el foco de la historia, que en ningún momento oculta que es parcial, subjetiva y, en algunos casos, falsa. Tony Wilson jamás escondió su pasión por las derrotas épicas ni la miseria moral de algunas de sus elecciones personales. No fue precisamente un marido ejemplar. Fallecido de un infarto en 2007, con 57 años, en una entrevista sobre la película definió su pensamiento en una frase: “Haz las cosas y ya luego descubrirás por qué las haces. En nuestro caso lo hicimos por puro amor a la música”.

items.title: 46-yr-old businessman commits suicide, leaves video message for family
items.description: By Dayo Johnson, Akure A 46-year-old businessman, Akinbolusere Kayode, has reportedly died by suicide in Ondo Town, Ondo State. Sources said he took his life in his office near BOVAS Petrol Station in Igba Town at about 3 p.m. on Thursday. Two empty bottles suspected to have contained poisonous substance were recovered by police detectives attached to the Bolorunduro Division who visited the scene. According to sources, the deceased recorded a video in which he spoke about his business challenges, humble beginnings, and relationship with his wife, whom he praised for standing by him throughout his struggles. He also repeatedly stated that no one pressured him into deciding to transfer his properties to his wife and three children. The state Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Jimoh Abayomi, confirmed the incident. Abayomi said the two empty bottles suspected to have contained Sniper insecticide were recovered from a nearby bush during the police investigation. He added that preliminary findings indicated that the deceased recorded a video before his death in which he lamented the hardships he faced in life. The video has since circulated widely on social media. His remains were evacuated and deposited at the State Hospital morgue for preservation and further examination. Police said no signs of foul play or visible injuries were observed on the body during the initial examination. The Commissioner of Police in the state, Felix Ohagwu, has ordered a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident to determine the actual cause of death. Ohagwu urged members of the public to refrain from speculation and allow investigators to carry out their work. He also advised individuals experiencing emotional distress, marital difficulties, or other personal challenges to seek timely support and assistance rather than resorting to actions that could endanger their lives. items.title: 2027: Obi not a threat in Lagos; we’ve corrected 2023 mistakes — APC
items.description: Chieftains of the All Progressives Congress, APC, in Lagos State said on Thursday that the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi, is not a threat in the state, as the mistake of 2023, when Obi won the presidential election in the state, has been corrected. The APC stalwarts stated this while fielding questions from journalists at the launch of the political movement established by the daughter of President Bola Tinubu and Iyaloja General of Nigeria, Dr. Mujidat Folasade Tinubu-Ojo, in Abuja. The movement, named the Iyaloja General Movement (IGM), is to mobilise votes for President Tinubu’s re-election in the January 16, 2027 presidential election. The Lagos State Director-General of the movement, Barrister Adejumbo Omofumilewa, said the inauguration served as a mini-rally in support of Tinubu ahead of the 2027 elections. Omofumilewa expressed confidence that the APC would perform better in Lagos State in the next presidential election, saying the party had addressed the factors that led to its loss in the state during the 2023 presidential poll. He attributed the outcome of the previous election to the party’s failure to adequately assess the political situation in Lagos, describing the experience as a betrayal. “What happened in 2023 that made our candidate lose the presidential election in Lagos State has already been taken care of, because now, everybody is following him,” he said. Omofumilewa also dismissed the prospect of opposition parties posing a serious challenge to the APC in Lagos, insisting that the ruling party had a strong presence across the state. “Obi is not a threat, neither is any party a threat in Lagos State. We are in charge,” he said, adding that the party was politically and organisationally positioned to secure victory in 2027. On his part, the Director-General of IGM, Dr. Nasiru Ladan, said the movement had already attracted over 2,500 support groups, with more organisations expressing interest. Ladan said the groups had been integrated into the movement’s structure and that the organisation was building a database of supporters across states and local government areas. “We have just started; it has been launched today, and we have machinery in motion in all the states, local governments, up to the ward level,” he said. He explained that the movement’s grassroots strategy was designed to translate its organisational structure into votes for the APC in 2027. According to him, the movement plans to deploy 10 facilitators to each polling unit, with each facilitator expected to mobilise 100 voters. He said the initiative was expected to help the movement achieve its target of 10 million votes, although he did not provide a breakdown of how the target would be measured or independently verified. The Lagos State Chairman of the APC, Cornelius Oyefolu Ojelabi, said the party was not leaving anything to chance in the forthcoming elections, as it attached great importance to them. “And you see that most of the political activities taking place now are centred on the All Progressives Congress. You will see them moving from one state to another,” he said. He further said: “You will see the All Progressives Congress moving from one local government to another. You will see series of support groups, in all ramifications, coming on board to show their solidarity and support for the presidential candidate of the All Progressives Congress. For the mere fact that we are the ruling party, we are not taking that for granted. “We are reaching out to the electorate. We are telling the electorate what this particular administration has been able to achieve and to consolidate on the achievements recorded in the last four years. So, we are not taking anything for granted. “And today, we are here to give our support to the Iyaloja General, who deemed it fit to bring the Iyaloja Generals in the whole country together to send the same message and let them take ownership of the forthcoming general election. “That is what we are known for, and that is what we have been doing. “And what happened during the 2023 election has strengthened us, because we know Lagos State has been the only state in the whole country that has been governed by one political party since 1999. So, what happened during the first election, to me, was a wake-up call. The Akwa Ibom State Coordinator of the IGM, Prince Mendy Achibong, said: “The movement in Akwa Ibom State is great. I want to say this: Iyaloja has come to stay in Akwa Ibom State, and we promise that in the 2027 election, Akwa Ibom State will give more than 80 per cent of its votes to our president, and it will be far, far more than the last election. items.title: 2027: How we will curb election violence — INEC
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, has unveiled an intelligence-led security framework to curb violence ahead of the 2027 General Election, vowing to hunt down anyone who threatens its ad-hoc staff, National Youth Service Corps NYSC members or permanent personnel. INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan SAN, disclosed this in Gombe on Tuesday while declaring open the North-East Zonal Interactive Meeting with Staff and Readiness Assessment for the 2027 General Election. The Commission in its daily bulletin said it was shifting from reactive, election-day deployments to a framework designed to protect voters, personnel and electoral materials before any ballot paper is moved. INEC said its collaboration with the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps NSCDC, the Department of State Services DSS, the Armed Forces and other paramilitary agencies under the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security ICCES has, according to him, been fundamentally restructured. The new framework, which the Commission terms the “ICCES Tentacle,” extends inter-agency security coordination from national and state headquarters directly down to the most remote Local Government Areas and Registration Area Centres. Amupitan told the gathering that no election, however well planned administratively, could be deemed credible if voters, election personnel and observers operate under physical threat or fear of violence. He explained that the framework rests on three pillars, the first being “Map and Mitigate.” Under it, the Commission will use Electoral Risk Management (ERM) tools to identify security flashpoints, seasonal threat factors and local vulnerabilities early, so that security agencies can deploy proactive measures long before ballot papers arrive. The second pillar, “Ensure Safety,” provides a protective umbrella over all electoral personnel, technological assets, including Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices and server infrastructure, and, most importantly, the voter. The third pillar, “Guarantee Access,” is aimed at ensuring that each of the 176,846 polling units nationwide remains a safe, peaceful and dignified space for the exercise of democratic rights, regardless of geographical remoteness or historical security challenges. According to him, the collaboration among the agencies had already produced concrete results. He disclosed that joint operations led by the DSS recently uncovered a covert plot by criminal kingpins targeting the Commission’s ad-hoc staff and Youth Corps members. Amupitan said swift, intelligence-led intervention neutralised the threat, and the principal orchestrators were arrested and are currently undergoing prosecution. “Let me send a clear message from Gombe,” Amupitan said, warning that anyone who attempts to threaten, intimidate or harm ad-hoc staff, NYSC members or permanent personnel of the Commission would be hunted down and brought to justice under the full weight of the law. He disclosed that the Commission would shortly convene a National Election Security Conference in Abuja, where state-specific security protocols for high-risk zones would be finalised. Amupitan acknowledged that the North-East presents distinct operational challenges, including vast desert terrains, riverine stretches along the Benue trough, remote agrarian communities and expansive landmasses. He noted, however, that the zone had demonstrated remarkable resilience and civic determination. The zone has 13,965,475 registered voters, representing 13.51 per cent of the national register of over 103 million. Bauchi State has the highest number with 3,012,547 voters, followed by Borno with 2,765,165, Adamawa with 2,431,146, Taraba with 2,254,380, Gombe with 1,768,566 and Yobe with 1,733,671. The Chairman said the 2027 General Election would be a simultaneous national undertaking across 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). The Presidential and National Assembly Elections are scheduled for Saturday, 16th January 2027, while the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly Elections will hold on Saturday, 6th February 2027. Earlier, the host Resident Electoral Commissioner REC for Gombe State, Alhaji Umar Muktar Gajiram, speaking on behalf of all North-East RECs, assured the Chairman that the zone was fully prepared, loyal and committed to ensuring that not a single voter out of the 13.96 million in the zone is disenfranchised. Gajiram said all directives on voter register display, logistics audit and technological testing would be executed to the letter. Amupitan assured staff and stakeholders across the North-East that INEC was not working in isolation, describing security as “the bedrock of electoral integrity.” “Insecurity may pose a challenge, but our collective constitutional resolve is far stronger,” he said. Aéroport Marrakech-Menara: hausse de près de 8 % du trafic des passagers à fin septembre
items.description: L’aéroport international de Marrakech-Menara a enregistré une hausse de 7,65 % du trafic des passagers en septembre 2026, par rapport au même mois de l’année précédente, portant à près de 9,88 % la progression cumulée du trafic à fin septembre, selon les données de l’Office national des aéroports (ONDA). Ainsi, cette plateforme aéroportuaire a accueilli 8.113.680 passagers durant les neuf premiers mois de l’année en cours, contre 7.383.977 voyageurs à fin septembre 2025, précise l’ONDA dans ses statistiques relatives au trafic aérien commercial au titre du mois de septembre 2026. Pour le seul mois de septembre dernier, l’aéroport Marrakech-Menara a accueilli 877.833 passagers, contre 815.468 voyageurs durant le même mois de 2025, soit une progression de 7,65 %. La ventilation du trafic aérien des passagers entre les vols nationaux et internationaux au titre du mois de septembre 2026 fait ressortir que le trafic international s’est établi à 837.349 passagers, contre 781.645 voyageurs en septembre 2025, enregistrant une hausse de 7,13 %. Le trafic national a, pour sa part, atteint 40.484 passagers, contre 33.823 une année auparavant, soit une progression de 19,69 %. Sur les neuf premiers mois de 2026, le trafic international à Marrakech-Menara a atteint 7.746.026 passagers, en hausse de 9,25 % par rapport aux 7.090.041 voyageurs enregistrés durant la même période de l’année précédente. Le trafic national s’est, quant à lui, établi à 367.654 passagers à fin septembre 2026, contre 293.936 voyageurs à fin septembre 2025, soit une augmentation de 25,08 %. S’agissant du Top 5 des routes aériennes internationales au titre du mois de septembre dernier, la liaison Marrakech-Menara-Paris-Orly arrive en tête avec 61.746 passagers, représentant une part de 7,37 %, suivie de la liaison Marrakech-Menara-Paris-Charles-de-Gaulle avec 53.778 voyageurs (6,42 %), Marrakech-Menara-Londres-Gatwick avec 37.480 passagers (4,48 %), Marrakech-Menara-Madrid avec 35.597 voyageurs (4,25 %) et Marrakech-Menara-Londres-Stansted avec 27.279 passagers (3,26 %). Au niveau national, les aéroports du Royaume ont enregistré, à fin septembre 2026, un trafic commercial de 29.330.764 passagers, en hausse de 8,74 % par rapport à la même période de l’année précédente. Pour le seul mois de septembre, le trafic aérien national s’est établi à 3.289.181 passagers, contre 3.040.171 voyageurs en septembre 2025, soit une progression de 8,19 %. items.title: Niger Illegal Miners: Detainees drank urine, sweat in NSCDC cell before 33 died – Report
items.description: Details have emerged of how alleged illegal miners held in a cell at the Niger State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) drank urine or sweat because they had no access to drinking water before 33 of them died. Read Also: Full List: Names of 37 miners who died in NSCDC custody In a report submitted by the Independent Investigation Committee, constituted by the Federal Ministry of Interior to investigate the deaths, it was discovered that the male cell had no running water and its toilet was not functioning. The report quoted survivors as describing how they experienced extreme heat, dehydration and overcrowding, while they were unable to move freely inside the approximately 12-square-metre cell. The Jonathan Kure-led 10-member committee authenticated 33 deaths occuring inside the male cell between 8 p.m. on 16 September and 7 a.m. the following day 17 September. The committee said the detainees had no drinking water, while officers ignored warnings about overcrowding and the risk of suffocation. According to the copy of the report obtained by PREMIUM TIMES, the deceased persons included 14 minors. The report, which painted a deplorable, harsh condition of the cell, stated that there were 41 survivors. It found that about 50 male detainees, including children, were confined in the cell, which had a solid metal door and inadequate ventilation. “The Committee finds that officers responsible for the cells failed to reduce the overcrowding, ignored prolonged cries and banging of the cell door and wall and did not provide emergency help,” the report said. Under the dehumanising condition of the male cell, the report said, there was “no water” and “toilet not functional”. It added that “detainees drank urine or sweat.” The situation in the female cell was barely better. The report said there was also “no drinking water” there, except from relatives. The toilet was also “non-functional but usable with fetched water,” according to the report. It added that relatives were prevented from bringing food to detainees on Wednesday, 16 September, the committee said. Warnings ignored The committee found that medical personnel had warned officers about the danger posed by the overcrowded cell before the deaths. Mariam Nelson, an NSCDC medical unit personnel, told the committee that she cautioned the cell guards, Usman Ndamaka and Hassan Mohammed, on the evening of 16 September that the overcrowding could cause suffocation. She said she advised them to leave the metal door unlocked to improve ventilation, but they ignored her warning. The report said detainees began experiencing symptoms, including eye irritation, burning throats, difficulty breathing, excessive sweating and intense thirst, from around 7:15 p.m. on 16 September. They subsequently began shouting for help and pleading for water. An armoury guard, Ahmed Abubakar Wushishi, told the committee that he heard persistent banging and screams from the cell between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. on 17 September. He said he approached the night guard, Hassan Mohammed, and urged him to open the cell. However, Mr Mohammed refused, citing an instruction from his superior, Mr Ndamaka, not to open the door without armed backup because the detainees might be planning an escape. According to the report, Mr Wushishi said the screaming stopped around 2:30 a.m. Mr Ndamaka admitted that he had instructed the night guard not to open the cell without armed backup. He also admitted that he did not respond to an emergency call from Mr Mohammed at 10:37 p.m. on 16 September, claiming he was asleep. He returned the call around 6 a.m. and arrived at the facility at about 7 a.m., when the cell was opened and the bodies discovered. The committee established that the deaths occurred inside the male cell between 8 p.m. on 16 September and 7 a.m. the following day. Children among detainees The report found that 14 of the deceased were minors. It also identified four children under the age of 14 who were recorded during profiling but were nevertheless placed in adult detention cells. The profiling officer, Abubakar Dabban, admitted that he had recorded four minors under 14 but processed them into the adult detention cells. The committee said this violated the children’s rights and applicable child-protection requirements. It also found that adults and minors were detained together in the overcrowded facility. Cause of deaths The committee attributed the deaths to acute hypoxic respiratory failure, also known as environmental asphyxia, worsened by heat stress and dehydration. However, it clarified that the medical conclusion was based on post-mortem examinations of only three available bodies. The other 30 had been buried before the medical team arrived. The report said the immediate cause of death was lack of oxygen, while the remote causes included failure of duty of care by NSCDC officers, poor detention infrastructure, inadequate emergency medical arrangements and weak institutional supervision. It rejected the claim that the deaths resulted from a disease outbreak, saying the available medical and forensic evidence did not support it. The committee recommended prosecution of officers found responsible, including for offences such as murder, criminal negligence, torture and inhuman treatment, where applicable. items.title: NDC must accept the same scrutiny demanded under Akufo-Addo — Afenyo-Markin
items.description: Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin has challenged the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) to uphold the accountability standards it championed during its eight years in opposition, insisting that a change of government must not shield public officials from scrutiny. He says the opposition will continue to question government expenditure, contracts and policy commitments, arguing that such oversight is a democratic responsibility rather than an attempt to undermine the administration. The Effutu MP’s remarks come amid growing controversy over the reported GH¢49.72 million expenditure on the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa. The Minority has raised concerns about alleged discrepancies in payment registers, duplicate entries and gaps in supporting documents relating to the exercise. It has called for an independent audit and demanded the resignation of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa. The opposition has also threatened to pursue a vote of censure against the minister if he remains in office. In a Facebook post on Friday, October 30, Mr Afenyo-Markin accused the NDC of adopting a different position on accountability since returning to power, saying the party should be prepared to face the same level of scrutiny it demanded of the previous New Patriotic Party (NPP) administration. “The NDC spent eight years teaching Ghanaians that questioning government was patriotism. Today, the same people appear offended that Ghanaians have taken those lessons seriously,” he wrote. Accountability debate Mr Afenyo-Markin argued that the NDC had previously scrutinised government contracts, challenged appointments, questioned public spending and demanded answers on policy promises. He said those actions were defended as necessary democratic oversight when the NPP was in office and should not now be dismissed as political persecution. “Apparently, accountability was a democratic virtue when the NPP was in power, but it has suddenly become political persecution now that the NDC occupies the seat of government,” he said. The Minority Leader maintained that the principles governing the use of public resources should remain unchanged, regardless of which political party controls the government. He stressed that public office carried an obligation to account to citizens and did not place ministers and other public officials beyond criticism. “Public office is not a personal possession; it is a public trust. Holding office does not grant anyone immunity from criticism. Questioning a contract is not a personal attack on the person who approved it. Demanding transparency is not an expression of hatred. Asking government to honour its promises is not an attempt to undermine it. It is simply democracy at work,” he said. Minority vows continued scrutiny Mr Afenyo-Markin said the Minority would not abandon its oversight responsibilities and would continue examining the government’s financial decisions and performance against its public commitments. “The Mighty Minority will continue to read the documents, examine the contracts, question public expenditure, and measure government promises against actual performance,” he said. He insisted that the NDC should be judged by the same standards it applied to the NPP while in opposition, adding that the Minority would not back down from demanding answers on matters of public interest. “The standard members of the NDC demanded when they were in opposition should be the same standard they must live by, and we, the Mighty Minority, will not renege,” he added. The dispute over the South Africa evacuation has intensified the political debate over public expenditure and the need for transparency in the management of state resources. The Minority’s concerns include the reported cost of the exercise and questions it says require independent examination of the supporting records.

It would cost around HK$1,000 (US$127.50) in Hong Kong, but only 300 yuan in Guangzhou and just 200 yuan in Zhongshan, two cities within two hours of Hong Kong. “Shenzhen is becoming less and less affordable,” said Leung, a retired vendor. items.title: Commuters risk life and limb as poles not removed from middle of road in Hyderabad
items.description: HYDERABAD: Carpeting of a new road and opening it for traffic, despite many electricity poles still standing in the middle of the dual carriageway, has triggered a heated debate on social media as travelers risk life and limb. Responding to the criticism from people, the Sindh government defended its decision to complete and open the road — connecting Alamdar Chowk with the old National Highway near Qasim Chowk — saying that the Hyderabad Electric Supply Company (Hesco) had been showing lethargy in fulfilling its responsibility of relocating the poles after which such a decision was taken. The poles carry high-tension lines emanating from near the 132-kV grid station of Qasimabad that feeds a considerably large part of Hyderabad city. Social media users had uploaded videos of the road dotted with the poles a couple of days back with crispy comments. CM says carriageway carpeted and opened to force Hesco into relocating transmission lines The poles existed in their place when the road was being given the first layer of carpeting. Since the two ends of the road were not blocked with barriers, vehicles started plying along it supposing that there was no risk in using it. However, the poles posed a great risk to commuters’ life. Motorists and bike-riders have to drive in a zig-zag manner to avoid hitting the poles. On Friday, the criticism forced Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah to publicly explain that it was Hesco’s responsibility to relocate the poles. The power utility was provided funds for the work, but it did not carry out the work, he said while speaking at the inaugural ceremony of the World Culture Festival in Karachi. The chief minister said there was a major issue of land availability for the construction of the road. The chief secretary, he said, contacted the military estate authorities and got the land use permission. He explained that as a matter of strategy, the government constructed the road first and restored the traffic so that pressure would come upon Hesco. He pointed out: “As soon as the road was constructed, public pressure increased and Hesco was forced to remove the poles”. The road is a 1.6km-long dual carriageway which is part of three road projects involving a cost of Rs1.06 billion. It is entirely new for the people of Hyderabad and connects the city’s bypass from the Qasim Chowk road. Until now used to be known as Ghora Ground, the artery has been converted to an asphalt road, the landscape otherwise being an abandoned waterlogged area used for electricity transmission to Deh Fouj Gah through the poles. The area is located within the administrative territory of the Cantonment Board Hyderabad and Military Estate Office (MEO). Chief Secretary Sindh Asif Hyder Shah had obtained permission from the two offices to build this road in order to lessen the traffic pressure on Qasim Chowk and Wadhu Wah in Qasimabad. The work on the road project had begun in April this year. Hyderabad mayor’s spokesman and district administration also had to respond to the criticism from people on social media. Sindh government’s spokesman Sadia Javed clarified the situation, but admitted that there was some sort of negligence seen on the part of the administration and that it should have put up barricades there with warning signs for commuters. “When development schemes are executed, some issues do crop up,” she maintained. According to Hesco spokesman Sadiq Kubar, Qasimabad grid station located near Alamdar Chowk feeds electricity to 27 feeders. Of them, 24 pass through this area which used to be an abandoned space until the road scheme was approved. He said that out of the 27 feeders, 22 have been shifted to new poles and accordingly energised. The remaining five would also be energized, he added. Similarly, he explained, 100 high-transmission lines needed to be shifted and out of them, 50 were positioned in the area until this road project was conceived. He said that relocation of the poles involved a cost of Rs79m. He said that while these 50 poles stood removed from the road, as many others were located along the grid station. Hyderabad Deputy Commissioner Zainul Abedin Memon, in his response to the issue on Thursday night, said that the road was not formally opened. He claimed that barricades, cautionary signage and other deterrents were deployed by the executive agency concerned and the traffic police, “but commuters continue to breach them daily”. He said proximity of Qasimabad grid station with the road necessitated relocation of electricity infrastructure, adding that until Wednesday (Oct 28), 97 poles had been shifted and the remaining ones would be relocated by Nov 10. He said only the ‘base binder course’ was laid; the final wearing (asphalt) course is yet to be laid. He said appropriate compaction is needed since it had previously been a waterlogged area. Thus, he added, ‘binder course’ is laid early. Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

items.title: Pharmacists warn against patronising street medicine vendors
items.description: •Say adulterated drugs can cause collapse of health sector By James Ogunnaike; Shina Abubakar & Deola Badru Pharmacists have warned Nigerians against patronising street medicine vendors following the growing threat posed by fake and counterfeit medicines in the country. Read Also: Deadly goods on sale: How fake products damage organs, destroy lives Speaking on the prevalence of counterfeit and substandard medicines in the country, they stressed that the problem poses serious risks to public health, including treatment failure, toxic reactions and potential damage to vital organs such as the liver and kidneys. They therefore called for stricter monitoring of medicines imported into the country, improved regulation of drug manufacturing and distribution and greater public awareness of the dangers associated with purchasing medicines from unauthorised sources. According to Pharm. Franklin Uzoezie: “Fake drugs, also known as counterfeit medicines, are products that do not meet the required standards or do not contain what they claim to contain. This could involve the active ingredient, the strength or dosage, or even the packaging. In some cases, a medicine may claim to contain a particular drug but contain none of it. In other instances, it may contain the drug but not in the correct quantity or strength. All these are examples of counterfeit or substandard medicines. The increasing circulation of fake and substandard medicines in Nigeria has become a major public health concern “The truth is that even healthcare professionals may find it difficult to distinguish between fake and genuine medicines just by looking at them. Their appearance, packaging and other features may be almost identical. In some cases, counterfeit products may even look better than the original medicines. Simply examining a medicine with the naked eye may not be enough to determine whether it is genuine or counterfeit. Appropriate laboratory analysis may be required to establish its composition and quality “When a medicine is counterfeit or substandard, it may contain the wrong ingredients, an incorrect quantity of the active ingredient, or potentially harmful substances. This can make the product ineffective or toxic to the body. The most important precaution is to know where you obtain your medicines. We often advise patients and members of the public not to buy medicines from just any place where they are being sold. Nigerians must purchase their medicines from licensed pharmacies and other legally authorised medicine outlets. “As patients and members of the public, we should not choose where to buy medicines solely because a seller offers a lower price or is conveniently located. We must prioritise the safety, quality and authenticity of the medicines we use. Purchasing medicines from approved sources, strengthening regulatory oversight and improving public awareness would help reduce the risk of exposure to counterfeit and substandard products”. Similarly, Pharm. Yetunde Akinola, Consultant Pharmacist and Pharmaceutical Care Specialist said, “The increasing circulation of fake and counterfeit medicines in Nigeria exposes serious weaknesses in the pharmaceutical supply chain and presents a grave danger to the health and safety of citizens. A counterfeit medicine is one that is deliberately and fraudulently misrepresented in terms of its identity, composition or source. Such products may contain incorrect ingredients, inadequate quantities of active pharmaceutical substances, no active ingredients at all or potentially harmful contaminants. There are also substandard medicines, which are authorised products that fail to meet the required quality standards. “The danger is that many of these products are packaged to look exactly like genuine medicines, making it difficult for unsuspecting members of the public to distinguish between them. Some counterfeit products even carry fake registration numbers and manufacturers’ details to deceive consumers. “One of the major factors encouraging the circulation of fake medicines is the patronage of unlicensed drug outlets, roadside vendors and unauthorised online medicine sellers. The desire to purchase drugs at cheaper prices also makes some Nigerians vulnerable to these fraudulent products. I would strongly advise members of the public to purchase medicines only from registered pharmacies and authorised medicine outlets. They should check product labels, expiry dates, batch numbers, packaging integrity and NAFDAC registration details. However, it is important to understand that these details can also be falsified, so checking them alone does not guarantee authenticity. “Pharmacists have a critical responsibility to ensure that medicines are sourced from legitimate and traceable distributors. They must maintain proper procurement records, observe professional standards and report suspicious products to the appropriate regulatory authorities. NAFDAC must strengthen its monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, particularly at ports of entry, distribution centres, open drug markets and other points where counterfeit medicines may enter the supply chain. There should also be stronger collaboration between regulatory agencies, pharmaceutical manufacturers, pharmacists and law enforcement organisations. “Beyond enforcement, there is a need for sustained public education. Nigerians must stop treating medicines as ordinary commodities that can be purchased from anywhere simply because they are cheaper or readily available. The quality and authenticity of a medicine can determine whether a patient recovers, suffers further complications or loses their life. Ultimately, the fight against counterfeit medicines requires collective responsibility. Government, regulators, healthcare professionals, medicine manufacturers and consumers must work together to ensure that only safe, effective and quality-assured medicines reach the Nigerian public”. On his part, Pharm. Adewuyi Ademola expressed worry that adulterated drugs could cause the collapse of the health sector. He argued that, “the end of every sickness is the drug prescribed by doctors when the right diagnosis is made. So, if the drugs are adulterated, the whole health sector will fail because drugs seem to be the last bus stop for everything. It is very important to ensure that we curb fake drugs from entering our country. “Generally, once there are no right drugs for patients to take, the whole health sector will collapse. Fake drugs means that the patients will not be getting well or getting what they are supposed to get. This can put a lot of pressure on the health sector, which will eventually increase the cost of providing healthcare to residents of the country”. Vanguard News The post Pharmacists warn against patronising street medicine vendors appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: SHC moved against construction on Karachi's Nehr-i-Khayyam
items.description: KARACHI: The Jamaat-i-Islami, along with some Clifton residents, moved the Sindh High Court against the provincial government for carrying out construction and development activities on Nehr-i-Khayyam. Leader of the Opposition in the City Council Advocate Saifuddin and three others filed a petition, citing the chief secretary, local government secretary, Karachi Metropolitan Corporation, Karachi Development Authority, Karachi Water & Sewage Corporation, Sindh Environmental Protection Agency and Boat Basin SHO as respondents. They submitted in the petition that they were aggrieved by the ongoing construction and development activities being carried out in and around Nehr-i-Khayyam in Clifton including adjacent amenity plots, which has raised serious concerns about preservation of the natural waterway, potential adverse impact upon city’s rainwater drainage system and the possible commercial utilisation of land of such waterway. They also contended that the construction, alteration and development were being carried out rapidly on the subject waterway and the mega project was being proceeded without a proper technical and environmental assessment, which may adversely affect the flow of rainwater, particularly during the monsoon season, thereby endangering public safety and the civic interests of residents of Karachi. They further stated that the respondents could not lawfully disregard the approved planning framework or permit development inconsistent with the designated purpose of the watercourse and its associated public infrastructure. Referring to previous judgements of the Supreme Court and the SHC, the petitioners maintained that the judiciary had stopped the construction in the vicinity of Nehr-i-Khayyam on a number of occasions, but after reported suspension of construction for a brief period, such activities had time and again been resumed. The petitioners maintained that if these construction activities were allowed to continue without lawful authority, adequate technical assessment and compliance with the applicable environmental safeguards, the same would threaten the effective functioning of an essential storm-water drainage facility and expose the residents to risks of flooding and environmental degradation. They asked the SHC to declare as illegal the alleged conversion, alteration or utilisation of the storm-water drain into a recreational park or commercial venture or any other inconsistent purpose without lawful authority and compliance with the applicable laws. They urged the court to preserve Nehr-i-Khayyam for its lawful purpose and primary function as a storm-water drainage channel. They also sought directives to immediately halt all ongoing construction and development activities and remove all structures, encroachments, unauthorised constructions, reclaimed portions and other works already erected or undertaken within the lawful boundaries of Nehr-i-Khayyam. Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

items.title: Deadly goods on sale: How fake products damage organs, destroy lives
items.description: *Everyday purchases now turn to health hazards *Patients end up paying twice for treatment —Adefunke Adeniyi *Counterfeit drugs damage kidneys, liver — Amarachukwu Enahoro *Adulterated drugs can cause collapse of health sector — Pharmacists warn By Chioma Obinna It is an understatement to say that Nigeria is currently battling a health crisis. Virtually every product, drug, food or drink is being counterfeited in the country and the consequence is fatal. Toddlers are no longer safe because counterfeit baby foods are everywhere. Parents now need to exercise caution in the choice of biscuits to give to their children as some biscuits have been discovered to contain toxic. A tablet swallowed to cure malaria could end up damaging the kidneys or liver while a bottle of drink bought to quench thirst could expose the consumer to dangerous substances. Similarly, cooking oil packaged under a trusted brand could contain ingredients far removed from what the label promises. For millions of Nigerians, the growing menace of fake and substandard products has turned everyday purchases into a potentially deadly gamble, with consequences ranging from failed treatment and organ damage to disability and death. The scale of the threat is underscored by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC), which reported destroying unsafe, falsified and non-compliant regulated products worth ₦22.73 billion between January and August 2026. Yet, beyond the billions of naira in seized and destroyed goods lies a more disturbing reality: the human cost of a trade that preys on consumers, undermines medical treatment, drains family resources and puts lives at risk. Health experts have therefore raised the alarm that harmful substances in counterfeit medicines, drinks and food products can damage vital organs. The question now is no longer just how much Nigeria is losing to fake products, but how many lives are being put in danger. When the medicine fails The danger is particularly serious when counterfeit or substandard medicines are used to treat common illnesses such as malaria. A patient experiencing fever and body aches may buy an antimalarial, take it as directed and expect to recover. But a medicine containing insufficient active ingredients, no effective ingredient or an inappropriate substance may fail to treat the illness, allowing the patient’s condition to worsen. Dr Amarachukwu Enahoro, a medical doctor and public health physician at Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH), said counterfeit medicines could defeat the very purpose for which they were purchased. “The consequence for that person might be that the main purpose for which this medicine was put, which is to treat malaria, will not be achieved,” she said. “The second implication is that it can now cause damage. Depending on what they used to prepare the fake medication, it can now cause damage to the kidneys and the liver.” The effects depend on the substances involved, the quantity consumed and the person’s health. While some injuries may be reversible with prompt treatment, severe damage can result in lasting loss of organ function, disability and a diminished quality of life. “The liver can be affected. The kidneys can be affected. And these have the potential to cause disability, loss of function, when these organs are damaged. It affects the quality of life of the people,” Enahoro said. A major NAFDAC operation in Lagos in February 2026 illustrated the potential scale of the threat. The agency reportedly seized more than 10 million doses of counterfeit malaria medicines and cosmetic products valued at approximately ₦3billion during a raid at Trade Fair Market. The reported haul included antimalarials, antibiotics and other medicines. Eight truckloads of products were removed, while four suspects were arrested. Another warning came in April 2025, when NAFDAC alerted Nigerians to counterfeit Aflotin 20/120 antimalarial tablets circulating under the name of a genuine medicine. The alert followed the identification of discrepancies in the counterfeit product’s packaging and batch information. For patients who depend on timely treatment, the danger is clear: a medicine may carry a familiar name without providing the quality, safety or effectiveness they expect. The danger beyond the medicine cabinet Counterfeit and adulterated food products can also expose consumers to harmful substances, sometimes affecting several people who consume the same product. Reports of deaths and hospitalisations following the consumption of locally made alcoholic and herbal drinks in Ondo State have raised concerns about the safety of beverages consumed at social gatherings. Reports have also linked suspected contaminated juices in Kano State to severe illness, including kidney-related complications. These incidents highlight the potential consequences when the contents and safety of products cannot be guaranteed. In January 2026, NAFDAC also reported an operation involving fake Goya Extra Virgin Olive Oil in Lagos. At Oke-Arin Market, Idumota, the agency reportedly uncovered an alleged operation in which palm oil was mixed with colouring agents and repackaged as Goya olive oil. The case illustrated how a trusted brand name could be exploited to sell a product whose composition differed from what consumers expected. For buyers, the deception may be difficult to detect. Familiar packaging can inspire confidence even when the contents have not been verified. Also speaking with Saturday Vanguard, Dr Ope Osunyomi, a public health expert, Financial Secretary of the Medical Guild and medical officer of health with the Lagos State Government, warned that harmful substances in fake products could damage vital organs. “If those things that they are consuming contain things that can affect those major organs of the body, it can actually lead to failure of those organs,” he said. The effects depend on the product’s actual composition, the amount consumed and the individual’s health. Children, pregnant women, older people and those living with chronic illnesses may be particularly vulnerable to certain harmful exposures. The difficulty is that consumers may not immediately recognise the connection between a product and their symptoms. Some counterfeit goods look convincing enough to inspire confidence, while copied labels and registration numbers can make them difficult to identify through visual inspection alone. Paying twice for treatment For many Nigerians, price plays a decisive role in what they buy. As household budgets tighten, cheaper medicines and other products can appear to offer much-needed relief. But a low price may conceal a much higher eventual cost. In a chat with Saturday Vanguard, Dr Adefunke Ronnie Adeniyi, a public health physician at LUTH, said consumers who bought fake or substandard products could end up spending more when the expected treatment failed. “The problem is that the cheaper product may not actually save them money in the long run,” she said. “If it is fake or substandard and the illness does not improve, they may end up spending more on another round of treatment, investigations or hospital admission.” A patient may need another consultation, additional medication or hospital admission. If complications develop, the costs can rise considerably. There is also the loss of income when illness prevents people from working. Families may have to divert money meant for food, school fees or other necessities towards treatment, while relatives may lose working hours caring for sick family members. Adeniyi said the problem should not be reduced to blaming consumers for purchasing cheaper products. Poverty and the rising cost of living can push people towards less expensive options, particularly where affordable, quality medicines are difficult to access. She also pointed to the complexity of the supply chain. Counterfeit products can enter through manufacturers, importers, wholesalers, markets, pharmacies and online sellers, making effective monitoring difficult. Some are packaged to resemble genuine products so closely that consumers cannot reliably distinguish them by appearance. Even a NAFDAC registration number is not conclusive proof of authenticity because counterfeiters can copy details from legitimate products. Consumers should buy medicines from reputable, licensed sources, check product details and use available authentication services. They should be alert to broken seals, altered labels and suspicious packaging, while remembering that visual inspection alone cannot guarantee safety. Anyone who suspects a product is falsified or contaminated should report it to the appropriate regulator. Those who become seriously ill after taking medicine or consuming a product should seek prompt medical attention and, where possible, retain the packaging and batch details to support investigation. The consequences also extend beyond individual households. Poor-quality antimicrobial medicines can contribute to treatment failure, while inadequate exposure to effective treatment can help resistant microorganisms survive and spread. Antimicrobial resistance makes infections harder to treat, potentially leading to longer illnesses, more complicated care and greater pressure on health facilities. According to Dr Adewale Oladipo, Medical Practitioner and Public Health Physician, “the increasing circulation of fake and counterfeit medicines in Nigeria is a serious public health threat that should not be treated lightly. The consequences go beyond the financial losses suffered by unsuspecting consumers; they directly threaten human lives. When people take counterfeit medicines, they expose themselves to serious health complications because such products may contain little or no active pharmaceutical ingredients, incorrect dosages or harmful substances. In some cases, patients may believe they are receiving treatment when, in reality, the drugs are doing nothing to address their medical conditions. “One of the most dangerous consequences is treatment failure. For instance, a patient suffering from malaria, typhoid, hypertension, diabetes or an infectious disease may experience worsening symptoms because the medicine being administered is either ineffective or contains the wrong ingredients. This can lead to complications, prolonged illness, organ damage and, in severe cases, death. “Another major concern is antimicrobial resistance, particularly with fake antibiotics. When medicines contain inadequate quantities of active ingredients, they may fail to eliminate disease-causing organisms, allowing them to develop resistance. This makes infections increasingly difficult and expensive to treat and poses a serious challenge to the healthcare system. The situation is particularly dangerous for children, pregnant women, elderly people and individuals living with chronic illnesses, who may suffer severe consequences from exposure to substandard or falsified medicines. “Nigerians must understand that taking medicines is not simply about swallowing tablets or administering injections; it is about ensuring that the products are genuine, safe and appropriate for the condition being treated. People should avoid self-medication, purchase medicines from reputable and licensed outlets, and seek medical advice whenever they experience unusual reactions or suspect that a medicine is ineffective. NAFDAC and other relevant authorities must also intensify public enlightenment, surveillance and enforcement to ensure that those involved in the production and distribution of counterfeit medicines are identified and prosecuted. Protecting the quality of medicines available to citizens is fundamental to protecting public health. From seizures to prevention The continued circulation of fake and substandard products calls for more than raids and destruction exercises. It requires a stronger system for detecting unsafe goods, tracing their sources and preventing them from reaching consumers. Osunyomi called for stronger regulatory institutions, particularly NAFDAC and the Standards Organisation of Nigeria, alongside more effective enforcement. “There’s a lot that needs to be done to help to strengthen these institutions, so that they can help to discover where some of these things are being done or being manufactured and being brought into the market space,” he said. Adeniyi called for more effective inspections, laboratory testing, surveillance and monitoring of distribution networks, including online sales. Manufacturers and distributors must maintain robust quality-control systems, while healthcare professionals should educate patients and report suspected falsified medicines or unusual treatment failures. Market associations can help discourage the sale of suspicious products, while law enforcement agencies should investigate those involved in large-scale production and distribution. Public education is equally important. Consumers need accessible information on how to purchase medicines safely, recognise warning signs and report suspected products. Government must also improve access to affordable, quality medicines so that cost does not push people towards unsafe alternatives. Osunyomi stressed that protecting communities cannot be left to regulators alone. “We need to take ownership of our community,” he said. She urged community leaders, religious organisations, market associations and individual citizens to reject the sale of unsafe products and report suspicious activities. The stakes are high. Beyond the value of goods seized or destroyed are the costs borne by families: money spent on repeated treatment, wages lost to illness, pressure on hospitals and the possibility of permanent injury. For Nigerians, buying medicine or food should not become a gamble with their health. A tablet should offer a genuine chance of recovery; a bottle of drink should not carry hidden dangers; and a familiar brand should mean what consumers have every reason to expect. The real measure of success in the fight against fake products will not be the value of goods destroyed, but how effectively Nigeria prevents unsafe products from reaching consumers.
