items.title: Pr. Nadine Machikou analyse les obstacles à l’application des décisions régionales
items.description: Lomé, 30 oct. (ATOP) – « La mise en œuvre des décisions des juridictions régionales africaines ne dépend pas uniquement des textes juridiques. Elle est également liée aux choix politiques des Etats, à leur organisation institutionnelle et à leur volonté de respecter les engagements pris au niveau communautaire ». C’est l’analyse faite par l’agrégée de sciences politiques, Pr. Nadine Machikou, à l’issue du colloque international consacré aux juridictions régionales africaines de protection des droits de l’homme, le vendredi 30 octobre à l’Université de Lomé. Abordant les difficultés d’application des décisions communautaires, Pr. Nadine Machikou a rappelé que la justice ne fonctionne pas en dehors du champ politique. Selon elle, les choix des autorités et les rapports de force au sein des institutions nationales peuvent influencer le sort réservé aux décisions des juridictions régionales. Elle estime donc nécessaire d’analyser conjointement les réalités judiciaires et politiques pour comprendre pourquoi certaines décisions sont appliquées, tandis que d’autres rencontrent des résistances. Les Etats ne réagissent pas toujours de la même manière selon la nature des questions concernées et les enjeux qu’elles soulèvent sur le plan intérieur. Pr Machikou a, par ailleurs, attiré l’attention sur la notion d’autonomie constitutionnelle, à laquelle les Etats restent attachés. « Cette autonomie leur permet de conserver une marge de liberté dans l’organisation de leur ordre politique et constitutionnel. La prise en compte de cette réalité est importante dans les relations entre les juridictions nationales et les instances régionales », a-t-elle souligné. Pour la politiste, l’exécution des décisions communautaires doit également être comprise à partir de la configuration politique de chaque pays : la composition des majorités, les rapports entre les institutions, la séparation des pouvoirs et le respect de l’Etat de droit. Autant de facteurs qui influencent la manière dont les décisions judiciaires sont reçues et appliquées. L’universitaire appelle ainsi à ne pas dissocier le fonctionnement des juridictions des réalités politiques nationales. Une meilleure compréhension de ces interactions, estime-t-elle, peut contribuer à renforcer le dialogue entre les juges et à améliorer l’application des décisions rendues par les juridictions régionales africaines. ATOP/AO/KYA

items.title: SIAO 2026: Ouagadougou, une terre de rencontres, de découvertes et d’opportunités
items.description: Le chef de l’Etat burkinabè, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, a ouvert, ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026, la 18 e édition du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO) qui se déroulera du jusqu’au 8 novembre. Une biennale qui fait de la capitale burkinabè une terre de rencontres, de découvertes et d'opportunités. Selon les organisateurs de l’évènement, ce sont plus 6 000 exposants et 800 000 visiteurs qui sont attendus à ce 18 e rendez-vous de la promotion de l’artisanat africain. Discours, coupure du ruban consacrant officiellement l’ouverture de la foire et des expositions, visite des stands, ont été les moments marquants de cette cérémonie d’ouverture. C’est parti pour la 18 e édition du Salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO). Le top départ de cette manifestation culturelle majeure qui se tiendra en dix jours et fera la capitale burkinabè le carrefour mondial de l’artisanat africain, a été donné par le guide de la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP), le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré himself. Cette édition comme les dernières contribuera à magnifier les artisans, ceux qui ont l’art chevillé au corps et l’intelligence de donner une autre vie, une autre forme, une autre expression de beauté à toute matière au bois, au bronze, au cuir, au coton, à l’argile. Ce Salon se tient dans un contexte où la souveraineté est la boussole de l’action politique. Cette 18 e édition mettra en exergue la puissance de la créativité et l’immensité du talent des artisans africains. Une vue des officiels de la cérémonie Ainsi, du 30 au 8 novembre prochain, les artisans africains venus de tous les horizons du monde, vont exposer leur savoir-faire et contribuer par-là à réaffirmer tout le talent qu’ont les Africains. Des vêtements aux chaussures en passant par les sacs à main aux produits de beauté et de décoration, tous les objets utiles à l’homme réalisés avec la main seront exposés au SIAO, la vitrine de l’artisanat africain, où un impressionnant dispositif sécuritaire, visible, rassure. Les dispositions idoines ont été prises par les organisateurs pour offrir un SIAO qui fera date aux populations burkinabè et africaines. Selon les organisateurs, ce sont plus de 6 000 exposants et plus 800 000 visiteurs qui sont attendus. Pour le président du Faso, ce Salon accueille une partie de l'Afrique et du monde, réunis autour de ce que l'humanité possède de plus précieux, le génie créateur du peuple, estimant qu’à travers les œuvres exposées, ce sont des siècles d'histoire, des civilisations, des traditions et des identités qui se rencontrent. «Par-delà nos frontières, nos langues et nos cultures, le travail demeure l'un des plus nobles langages de l'humanité», a affirmé le ministre chargé de l’Artisanat, Serge Gnaniodem Poda qui a lu le discours d’ouverture du Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré qui a salué particulièrement la République du Ghana, pays invité d'honneur, ainsi que les Républiques du Mali et du Niger, pays invités spéciaux, dont les liens profonds d'histoire, de fraternité et de destin, ont unis et réunis au sein de l’Alliance des Etats du Sahel (AES). Visite des expositions après l'ouverture officielle du Salon Depuis sa création en 1988, le SIAO s'est progressivement imposé comme l'un des grands rendez-vous de la créativité africaine, devenant bien plus qu'un espace d'exposition et de commerce. Il est le lieu où le continent africain présente au monde son intelligence, son identité et l’extraordinaire capacité des africains à transformer la matière en beauté, en utilité et en richesse. «Derrière chaque étoffe tissée, chaque objet sculpté, chaque ouvrage façonné, il y a une histoire humaine. Il y a le geste patient d'un artisan, la mémoire d'une communauté, le savoir transmis par un père, une mère ou un maître à son apprenti. Ces femmes et ces hommes ne demandent pas la charité», a affirmé le président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoro dans son discours. Selon le père de la RPP, les artisans demandent que leur travail soit reconnu, que leur talent soit valorisé et que leur génie puisse leur assurer une existence digne. «Notre reconnaissance serait incomplète si elle ne s'accompagnait pas d'une ambition à la hauteur de leur contribution. Comment accepter que notre continent, si riche de talents, de matières premières et de savoir-faire, demeure encore largement dépendant de l'extérieur pour satisfaire ses propres besoins ? Cette contradiction doit désormais interpeller notre conscience collective», a-t-il soutenu. Pour lui, le thème de cette 18e édition: «Artisanat africain et industrialisation: quelle synergie pour une meilleure organisation et valorisation des produits locaux et du patrimoine culturel», invite précisément chaque Burkinabè et africain à relever ces défis historiques. «Pour nous, la réponse est claire. L'artisanat ne doit plus être considéré uniquement comme l'héritage de notre passé», a fait savoir le capitaine Traoré. Le président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré Selon le président Traoré, l’art doit devenir l'un des fondements de l’avenir industriel des pays africains. «L'industrialisation de l'Afrique doit prendre racine dans nos réalités, nos ressources, nos besoins et nos savoir-faire, sans reproduire aveuglement des modèles conçus ailleurs. Nous devons permettre à l'artisan qui travaille aujourd'hui dans un modeste atelier de devenir, demain, le responsable d'une unité de production moderne, capable d’employer des jeunes et de conquérir des marchés internationaux», a-t-il soutenu, faisant observer qu’il ne s'agit pas d'opposer la tradition à la modernité, mais de mettre la modernité au service de du génie ancestral africain. «C'est ainsi que nous transformerons notre patrimoine culturel en puissance économique, sans jamais lui faire perdre son âme. Cette ambition est au cœur de la Révolution progressiste populaire que nous conduisons au Burkina Faso. Notre révolution ne se limite pas à la reconquête de notre territoire. Elle porte également l'exigence de reconquérir notre capacité à produire, à transformer, à inventer et à décider librement de notre avenir. Nous sommes convaincus qu'aucune souveraineté politique ne peut durablement prospérer sans souveraineté économique», a dit Serge Poda, qui a lu le discours du chef de l’Etat du haut de la tribune dressée sur un podium géant qui accueillera beaucoup de manifestations culturelles, notamment les arts de scènes, les soirées pour égailler les exposants et les visiteurs. Le ministre chargé de l'Artisanat, Serge Poda Pour le président Ibrahim Traoré, son ambition affichée de donner une place de choix dans le concert des nations au savoir-faire africain dépasse les frontières du Burkina Faso. «Elle rejoint les aspirations de la Confédération des Etats du Sahel et au-delà, celles de tous les peuples africains qui entendent prendre pleinement leur place dans le marché mondial. L'Afrique ne manque ni de ressources, ni d'intelligence, ni de créativité. Ce qui lui a trop souvent manqué, ce sont les conditions qui lui permettent de transformer ses immenses potentialités en une prospérité véritablement partagée», a-t-il déclaré. Il a, par ailleurs, invité la jeune génération africaine à corriger cette injustice historique en développant des chaînes de valeurs africaines, en renforçant les échanges entre leurs pays et en créant des marchés capables de soutenir les producteurs du continent, considéré comme le berceau de l’humanité. Aux artisans, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, appelé affectueusement «IB», leur dédient cette édition du SIAO. «Je connais les sacrifices que représentent vos métiers, les longues heures de travail, les difficultés d'accès aux équipements, aux financements et aux marchés. Mais je connais également votre persévérance et votre immense contribution à la vitalité de nos économies. Je vous invite à croire davantage à vos capacités, à vous organiser, à transformer vos connaissances et à rechercher sans cesse l'excellence», leurs a-t-il lancé à travers son ministre de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat, Serge Poda. Aux industriels, aux investisseurs et aux institutions financières, le chef de l’Etat burkinabè, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, leur demande de regarder les artisans africains autrement, non comme de simples bénéficiaires d'assistance, mais comme des partenaires économiques porteurs d'un potentiel considérable. «À notre jeunesse, je dis ceci, n'ayez jamais honte de vos mains ni des métiers hérités de vos parents. Un peuple qui méprise ses propres savoir-faire finit par dépendre de ceux des autres. Apprenez, perfectionnez vous, innovez et osez entreprendre. L'avenir de l'Afrique se construira aussi dans l'intelligence d'un jeune créateur, dans la persévérance d'une tisseuse, dans l'habileté d'un sculpteur et dans l'audace d'un entrepreneur qui décide de produire sur sa propre terre», a-t-il conclu sur la vision qu’il porte sur l’artisanat avant de réaffirmer que pendant les dix jours de la 18 e édition du SIAO, la capitale burkinabè sera une terre de rencontres, de découvertes et d'opportunités. Il a donc formulé le vœu que ce rendez-vous culturel ne soit pas seulement celle des belles expositions et des discours promoteurs, mais celle des engagements concrets, des partenariats durables et des perspectives nouvelles pour les artisans. La représentante du pays invité d’honneur, Ghana, Élisabeth Afosu-Adjaré, ministre du Commerce, de l’Agrobusiness et de l’Industrie, a soutenu que «le secteur de l’artisanat est une source d’opportunité pour (les) populations et c’est pourquoi le Ghana adhère pleinement au thème de la 18 e édition du SIAO». Elle a fait noter que son pays est présent au SIAO avec une forte délégation composée, entre autres, de représentants du gouvernement, d’artisans et d’entreprises issus des 16 régions du Ghana. Et à ce rendez-vous d’affaires et d’opportunités, le Ghana présentera des créations uniques, authentiques et de classe mondiale, a-t-elle laissé entendre. La coupure du ruban marquant l’ouverture officielle de l’évènement suivi de la visite des expositions ont été les derniers actes de la cérémonie. Par Bernard BOUGOUM L’article SIAO 2026: Ouagadougou, une terre de rencontres, de découvertes et d'opportunités est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Agroécologie paysanne : vers la tenue d’une première foire africaine
items.description: Au terme de cinq jours d’échanges à Niaguis, dans le département de Ziguinchor. des réseaux africains engagés dans la promotion de l’agroécologie paysanne affichent leur volonté de renforcer leur coopération. Parmi les principales perspectives retenues figure l’organisation d’une foire africaine destinée à promouvoir les produits agroécologiques et à faire de cette pratique un levier de souveraineté alimentaire. ZIGUINCHOR – Faire de l’agroécologie paysanne un mouvement continental plus fort et mieux organisé. C’est l’une des principales ambitions qui se dégagent de la conférence internationale organisée pendant cinq jours à Niaguis. Cette rencontre, qui a réuni des participants venus de 23 pays d’Afrique et d’Amérique, avec dix réseaux africains engagés dans les questions agroécologiques, ouvre de nouvelles perspectives de collaboration. Au cœur de celles-ci, un projet ambitieux : l’organisation d’une foire africaine autour de l’agroécologie. À la clôture des travaux, Mamadou Danfakha, coordonnateur du mouvement panafricain « Nous sommes la solution » et chargé de programme à Fahamu Africa, une association panafricaine engagée dans la justice sociale, s’est réjoui de la qualité des échanges. Pour lui, cette première rencontre africaine doit surtout permettre aux différents réseaux de rapprocher leurs démarches et de construire une action commune. A lire aussi : Agroécologique paysanne : à Ziguinchor, 23 pays africains unis pour changer les pratiques culturales « Nous sommes satisfaits des réflexions menées durant ces cinq jours. L’enjeu est désormais de renforcer les liens entre les réseaux et de mieux coordonner leurs interventions en faveur de l’agroécologie paysanne », a-t-il expliqué. Parmi les perspectives annoncées, l’organisation d’une foire africaine occupe une place particulière. L’initiative vise à créer un cadre de rencontre, d’exposition et de partage autour des productions agroécologiques. « Au lieu de travailler chacun de son côté, nous voulons nous retrouver régulièrement pour conduire des actions communes, plus fortes et plus mobilisatrices. Nous avons ainsi évoqué la possibilité d’organiser une foire africaine de l’agroécologie, une première à l’échelle du continent », a précisé Mamadou Danfakha. Vulgariser davantage l'agroécologie Au-delà de son caractère commercial, cette foire ambitionne de mieux faire connaître les produits issus de pratiques agricoles respectueuses de l’environnement et de sensibiliser les décideurs à leur potentiel. « Une telle initiative permettra de vulgariser davantage l’agroécologie et de montrer aux pouvoirs publics qu’elle constitue une véritable réponse aux défis de la souveraineté alimentaire. Elle peut également réduire notre dépendance aux engrais chimiques et aux produits de synthèse », a-t-il souligné. Des espaces d’exposition de produits biologiques, cultivés sans traitements chimiques, sont envisagés. Cette volonté de mutualiser les expériences est également saluée par Mamadou Goïta, directeur exécutif de l’Institut de recherches et de promotion des alternatives en développement, venu du Mali. Il voit dans cette rencontre la naissance d’un espace permanent de coopération et d’apprentissage collectif. « Nous sommes heureux de voir émerger un cadre dynamique qui favorisera la convergence des idées, le partage des expériences et la collaboration. L’objectif est de permettre à chaque réseau de renforcer les initiatives engagées dans son pays et dans sa région », a-t-il indiqué. Avec le projet de foire africaine en perspective, les participants entendent donner une plus grande visibilité aux productions paysannes et faire de l’agroécologie une réponse concrète aux défis alimentaires du continent. Gaustin DIATTA (Correspondant)

items.title: The Internet Might Need to Be Rebuilt From Scratch
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube AI hacking swarms are poking holes across the internet at such a rate that some cybersecurity professionals have dubbed this month “Black October.” The AI-cybersecurity professional Alex Stamos argues that it’s time to be proactive rather than reactive, and that might mean rewriting the code for the internet in newer programming languages that could make all of our online systems and personal information safer. He joins the Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel to explain why that’s not as big of a deal as it sounds, and how we can all protect ourselves in the meantime. The following is a transcript of the episode: Alex Stamos: What we have to do, as people who work in cybersecurity, is: We have to shorten the Dark Age. We need to make sure the Library of Alexandria doesn’t burn, right? We have to do everything possible to make this as short as possible. And from my perspective, the best way to do that is to be proactive, not reactive, here. And to be proactive we can’t just wait for these bad things to happen; we have to intentionally re-architect things. Charlie Warzel: It’s late October. There’s an upcoming election. There’s a World Series. There’s this endless string of bracing news events. But there’s another crisis looming as well. The digital infrastructure that powers our entire on- and offline lives is, according to the people who protect it, more vulnerable than ever. The internet as we know it is a very fragile ecosystem. So much of it is built off of code that’s written by humans—that is, by nature, full of flaws or bugs. Some of our critical digital infrastructure, it’s built off of decades-old technology that’s running on ancient code languages. The internet is a marvel. But it is also, like any massive human endeavor, imperfect and full of vulnerabilities. One way to look at the history of cybersecurity is as a race between people who are looking to exploit all those vulnerabilities and the people who can fortify our systems and keep them secure. But in recent months, AI has threatened to change the dynamics of that race. AI agents—which are cheap, relentless, and highly capable hacker armies—are proving excellent at finding vulnerabilities in code. Sometimes, oftentimes, in places that humans had never thought to look. And the result has been this series of high-profile cybersecurity incidents, each one adding to this feeling that we’ve entered a new era. The rate of disclosures of incidents has been so intense that in recent weeks, cybersecurity professionals are referring to this month as Black October. Last week, the public found out that AI agents found vulnerability in PHP, which is a coding language that affects 70 percent of the internet, that could allow hackers to gain access to almost any server. On top of PHP, there have been disclosures in major software products like Node.js, which is software that’s used across countless important webpages and services on the internet. This is stuff that powers everything from supply chains to health-care companies. And the fear is that what we are seeing here is not some kind of aberration, but the beginning of this new normal—this period of time where everything from our power grids to our personal data may be uniquely vulnerable. And so I wanted to understand exactly how unprecedented this Black October moment really is, and what it means for the state of the internet and the possibilities of catastrophic events in the future. Alex Stamos is the chief information security officer at the AI company Cognition, and the former chief security officer at Facebook. He is not only on the forefront of this current crisis, but he’s also somebody who understands how massive digital organizations respond to the demands of an increasingly insecure internet. I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . [ Music ] Warzel: Alex Stamos, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Stamos: Hey, thanks for having me, Charlie. Warzel: So we’re in the middle of what feels right now like this explosion of either AI-powered hacks or cybersecurity disclosures. Right now, people in your industry, and colloquially on places like X are referring to it as Black October. Pretty ominous. Can you walk me through what has changed fundamentally in the last two weeks? Stamos: Yeah. So we’re just kind of—this has honestly been a slow burn. But what’s been really interesting in this month is that finally attackers are getting the benefit from AI; where they have the ability to use AI to automate what we call kill chains . So you know, this is a term we have stolen from the military—where, when the military says “kill chain,” they mean to actually kill something. In the cyber world, those are the steps you take to break into a network and to do something. And traditionally, you could automate some parts of a kill chain. But there’s often human steps. And just in the last several months, we’ve gotten to the point of where AI models—and especially the open-weight models, the models that you can run locally on hardware you run yourself, and even commodity hardware like these new Mac Studios that you can buy—are good enough that basically every step of the kill chain can be completely automated with AI. And so that has really changed the game here—where you can get rid of any human bottleneck. And that has completely changed the economics and the speed at which attackers can move. Warzel: So I’ve heard of this being talked about as a “disclosure wave,” meaning that it’s a disclosure of potential vulnerabilities and not a wave of attacks. But what’s the truth to that? Stamos: Yeah, I don’t think that’s true. We’ve actually had a wave of attacks, but it’s way before this October. We’ve had a building wave of attacks over the last year or so as attackers have automated their kill chains. There’s a good thing happening, which is—these vulnerabilities have existed for decades, right? We have, you know, years and years and years of human-written code that is not reliable, that is not safe. That is often written in languages that are not what we call memory safe and type safe, that are written in computer languages that were not fundamentally easy to write safe code in. Languages like C and C++. And unfortunately, it turns out that human beings writing code in those languages—it’s very hard to make systems that are safe in the presence of these superhuman bug-finders. And so what’s happening is we are now burning through all of these bugs that were written over two decades, and they are being found and discovered and patched. But the problem is, once those patches are released, actually getting them fixed in the wild takes a while. And so bad guys have a window during which they can then exploit them. And over the last year, we have seen that exploitation happening. Sometimes manually, and more and more automatically. And so yes—we have seen waves and waves of exploitation. It’s not being covered as much, but it is extremely hard if you have a security emergency on a Friday evening. And it’s often on a Friday evening; unfortunately, that’s how it often seems to work out. It is very hard to get professional incident responders on the phone, because everybody is booked up pretty far out right now. Warzel: So all of this news, as an outsider, is really bracing to just see come across the timeline. I don’t think it’s very clear for a lot of us without the expertise to evaluate some of these claims. The one that I saw the other day that I wanna bring up here is the reports that the cloud service from Japan’s GMO Internet Group, which is used also by financial traders, had been hacked. And in one report that I saw circulating, the CEO of GMO suggested that the internet as we know it could be on the verge of collapse due to this pressure. When we hear something like that, how are we supposed to evaluate that kind of claim? What is the state of the internet right now? Stamos: Oh, so to say the internet is going to collapse, I think, is hyperbole. The fundamental infrastructure of the internet is holding up fine, right? Like the internet—the routers, the switches—there have been bugs in the fundamental systems that move traffic, but those have been fixed. I think what is happening, however, is we have lived through a period where you have been able to assume that if you use a service, that your data is going to be safe. That assumption was never correct, it turns out. Right? The systems were never safe. It’s just that we lacked the number of skilled attackers to take advantage of the fundamental insecurity of these systems. And what is happening now is the bugs are being found. Sometimes by the bad guys, often by the good guys. But in the period in which it takes for the bugs to be fixed, the bad guys have an opportunity to take advantage of that period of time, of that lag of fixing them. And then the bad guys—the skill sets. You know, I don’t know if you’re an English soccer/football fan, but everybody gets this metaphor now ’cause they watch Ted Lasso . But you know, right, so the English football leagues—if you do really well, you get sent up, right? If you do poorly, you get relegated; you get sent down. Well, what’s happening is: Every attacker is now getting sent up a league, right? And so you know, it used to be the Premier League was just a handful of really big countries—so the United States and our allies—called the Five Eyes. So the United States, the U.K., Canada, Australia, New Zealand, is called the Five Eyes. Russia, China, Israel, a couple other Western nations were up there at the top. And then you had the next tier—which was like Iran, North Korea, a couple other second-tier countries. And then you had the really good independent professional commercial groups. And what’s happening is everybody’s going up a league, because of AI. Which in some ways is bad for the people at the top, because they’re losing their premier status. That everybody else is kind of joining them. The skill sets that used to be really unique are becoming much less unique because of AI. And so I think that’s what we’re seeing now. That skills like taking a patch from Microsoft and reverse-engineering it and turning it into exploit code? Maybe 150, 200 people used to be able to do that five years ago. Now, a 19-year-old in St. Petersburg can do that with a M5 Mac Ultra. That’s kind of—and that’s really crazy. Warzel: There’s a striking anecdote that I’ve seen floating around: that the PHP vulnerability that, you know, affected 70 percent of websites on the internet was independently discovered by someone using a frontier model, using the prompt “Find bad vulnerabilities in PHP.” And I think that sort of speaks to that idea, right? That everyone is elevated; everyone has these skills they didn’t have. But if people without even real basic knowledge of these systems or skills can do this, how is this sustainable for, you know, cybersecurity? Stamos: Yeah. So what’s going to have to happen—like you said, what’s happening is, you have these bugs that will be found by somebody with access to a preview version of a cyber model. We do this thing called “coordinated disclosure,” where sometimes if you have a really big bug like that, it used to be you could wait 90 days. But in those 90 days, the models might get better, that everybody has access to, that you can’t wait, right? Because other people can just find the bug. So the way we’re gonna get through this is—I think what we’re gonna have to do is we’re gonna have to rewrite a bunch of code. So I actually gave a talk earlier this year where I posited two scenarios, which is the good and the bad scenario. And the good scenario was that there was a finite number of bugs, and we were just burning them down. And we would asymptotically approach. As new models came out, you’d have fewer and fewer. And the bad scenario was every time we have a new model, you get the equal number of bugs. Unfortunately, we’re closer to the bad scenario still. Which is: Every time one of these new models comes out, we still have a huge number of incredibly complex memory-management flaws. And so I think for these really complex code bases, we’re going to have to refactor them. We’re going to have to rebuild them in languages like Rust, where you have the ability to, one, there’s entire classes of bugs they don’t have. And then you also have the ability to effectively have kind of contracts where you say “I am designing it to have these properties,” and you can mathematically prove that it has those properties. There’s a thing called formal verification. And you don’t have to do true formal verification, which is really hard, and it would’ve been basically impossible to do this with humans. Or incredibly expensive. But with LLMs, you can. And so I think we’re just gonna have to basically completely rewrite stuff. And that is actually going to be cheaper with AI than it’s going to be to do 1,000 bugs every six months. We should just redo these things. Warzel: But let’s talk about that. Like how long does something like that take, a rewriting the code of the internet? Stamos: Well, less time than you might think. I think that’s actually one of the things that’s changed with AI. So I work at this company called Cognition now, and we have a product called Devin. And we work with companies, and we have these examples; like, we worked with Mercedes-Benz, and we rewrote one of these apps of theirs that would’ve taken months and months for humans to do. And we did it in like eight days. So I think actually this is one of those beliefs that software engineers have—that it’s impossible to do this. And it’s actually quite plausible. Warzel: I’ve also heard you say, and maybe these are the same thing, but I’ve heard you say that we’re entering a dark age of cybersecurity. Is that what you mean by that? And that sounds really kinda ominous. Stamos: Yeah. I mean, we are. I’ve gotten a little crap for this, and maybe that’s deserved. But like, the Dark Ages—we came out of them, right? So first off, the Dark Ages were only for part of the Earth. Like, the Dark Ages happened in Europe, and things were, like, fine in China. You know, things were great. They had a flourishing civilization. But in Europe, we had Greek and Roman civilization, and then things got kind of rough for a while. And we forgot about a lot of things. But then we had the Enlightenment, and we had the Renaissance. And so my point is that what we have to do, as people who work in cybersecurity, is: We have to shorten the Dark Age. We need to make sure the Library of Alexandria doesn’t burn, right? We have to do everything possible to make this as short as possible. And from my perspective, the best way to do that is to be proactive, not reactive, here. And to be proactive is: We can’t just wait for these bad things to happen. We have to intentionally re-architect things. We have to intentionally rewrite things. We have to intentionally change how we do cybersecurity. We have to intentionally change how we build the networks. We have to intentionally change how we build security teams. Right now, we’ve been very reactive. We still do patching like we did five years ago. Most security teams are still built like they were built five years ago. Like: The jobs are the same, the defensive structures are the same, how we do incident response is the same. And I think that’s a problem. And when I say “shorten the Dark Age,” what I mean is, we’ve kind of gotta actually utilize AI to proactively—we’ve gotta to make this better. Otherwise, we’re just going to try to patch-patch-patch our way through it. And that’s not gonna work. Warzel: In the scenario you’re describing—rewriting things with today’s better code—do we just end up, if we do that, in the same situation later? When more powerful AI models find these new vulnerabilities? Or that the code, you know, allows for these, like, superhuman-style bugs that we are incapable of kind of comprehending? Is that a possible scenario? Stamos: I don’t think so. I mean, it’s hard. Now we’re getting to, like, metaphysics, when you talk about like these superhuman capabilities. But I don’t think so. I think if we start rebuilding things using languages that eliminate these entire classes, and then you start using some level of formalism, then it’s much less likely that’s true. Certainly what we’re doing right now is not working, right? I just think it’s total malpractice to write anything in C and C++. Any company that is shipping code that is written in C++ in 2027 is, from my perspective—that is just completely inappropriate. Warzel: And for the people listening who aren’t as familiar, the reason for that is just ’cause it’s an old, outdated language. And you just don’t wanna have your systems be running off that. It’s easier to exploit all that, right? Stamos: Right. Because the language C++—C and C++ are languages from the 1980s. The ’70s actually, and 1980s. And in fact, in the original book for the C programming language—which I was taught at Berkeley out of this book, in the original printing—there was a security flaw in the book that was written by the original authors of the language, right? Kind of famously. You can make mistakes, because these languages are what’s called low level. And you have to intentionally decide how you talk to the processor, and how you handle memory. And so a lot of the kind of fundamental flaws that we see that get exploited these days is about deciding how you manipulate memory, the memory of the computer. You say, “I want to allocate memory. I wanna deallocate memory.” And the bugs that we see, like the PHP bug, these are memory-allocation errors. In modern languages, these things are handled for you automatically. And in really modern languages, like Rust, you have the ability to say not just it handles the memory for you, but you can effectively say to the compiler—the software that takes what you say and then turns it into the language the computer actually executes. You can say, “This is what I intend. This is what I want to happen.” And so there’s double-checks, triple-checks to make sure bad things don’t happen. Now, that would’ve been totally improbable in the 1980s, ’cause computers weren’t fast enough. It would’ve made the computers way too slow. But computers are incredibly fast now, and so these languages are much slower. But who cares? Because computers are spectacularly fast. We have way, way more speed, and so we sacrifice a little bit of speed for a lot more safety. And it would’ve been completely improbable to rewrite Windows, to rewrite Linux, to rewrite the Cisco kernel code—to rewrite all of the stuff that powers all of the electricity, the light that you and I, that’s shining on us. All of the little processors that power the hydroelectric plant that’s—you know, ’cause you’re in the Pacific Northwest, you’re probably getting hydropower from Washington and Oregon and British Columbia. I’m getting wind power and solar power in California. Those systems are from PLCs [programmable logic controllers]; from Siemens and Schneider Electric and companies like that. That’s all written in C code. That stuff could be rewritten in Rust now. It just means you have to pay to replace that stuff. It will cost money, but that is worth it for our society to continue to operate over the next decade. And I think that’s worth it, but we have to proactively decide as a society to do that. Warzel: So let’s talk about that. You obviously mentioned, like, power-grid systems. Some of this very foundational infrastructure, running off of some of this old stuff. We need to do something about it. You also said early on that people are overwhelmed, right? That there’s so much happening. Do we have the resources to do this in an orderly fashion? To respond to the level of the threat right now? Because I think what I am seeing is these concerns from people—perhaps they’re just engagement farming on places like Twitter, but they’re talking about vulnerabilities to the power grids. They’re talking about vulnerabilities to these very critical pieces of infrastructure. Stamos: I mean, what do you mean by the resources? Certainly, so, one—Twitter’s not real life. I think that has to be one of the most important things that we have to remember, right? Like, the capability absolutely exists, because modern AI systems have the ability to do this. What we haven’t done is created the incentive structure. First, for the people who run the power grid to put the pressure on their vendors, and for the vendors who build these things to build systems this way. And the economic structures for us to actually upgrade all this stuff. We haven’t created those economic incentives yet. Warzel: Isn’t the incentive structure for the power grids that you don’t want someone to find a vulnerability—you know, the 19-year-old in St. Petersburg—and take down the power grid? Like, aren’t we there? It feels to me like we’re there. Stamos: Yeah. So, okay. I mean, I do a lot of work with some infrastructure providers. And of all the infrastructure providers, the power companies are actually the best. It’s—one, they’re quite large. Like, we’ve seen all these attacks against water utilities. And they’re, for example, in much worse shape, because they’re much smaller organizations. They’re often municipalities. A lot less time and money has been spent on water, for example, or sewer systems. So you’re right—power is the best shape, and they do have the economic incentive. I think there’s still a bunch of coordinated action issues, in that there has not been enough work by them to put pressure on the vendor ecosystem to do all the right things. So yes; the power-grid people have done good work here. But most of the work they have done is in isolation, right? So effectively, how they have done security is: They have basically decided that the stuff they buy is crap, and that they will make sure that attackers have no ability to reach it. That is a reasonable protective strategy for now, because that is all they can do. But in the long run, we need to rebuild these systems, and we need to make them safer. Because against the right adversaries, you can’t actually physically isolate a power grid. Because against adversaries who are advanced enough, they will physically infiltrate and send somebody up the power pole and then tap into that physically isolated network. And I think people spend too much time on the power grid, ’cause it is the thing that worries everybody. There’s a lot of other things that, if they go down—like hospitals. Like, hospitals get slaughtered all the time by ransomware actors, right? And those things are really critical, and they’re also very hard things to disconnect, because we all have electronic medical records, right? And especially community hospitals. Things run by counties are extremely poorly resourced compared to things like the power grid, from a security perspective. Warzel: What are some of the things that you have seen in recent months—either the disclosures or the actual attacks—that have you the most concerned right now? Stamos: Yeah. So, I mean, I think a couple of things that were really interesting and indicative of where we’re going. First, there were these attacks against South Korean banks. Warzel: Mhm. Stamos: Using fully automated AI-attack systems called Artex. So they’re these AI-attack systems that use open-weight models to do all of the attacks. There’s a thing called Voyager that was released earlier this year, or late last year, that would do AI-enabled attacks, but those were mostly used for kinda low-level stuff. So if this stuff is now at the point where you can do a full attack against a bank in a technologically advanced country, then we’re really kind of there. And so we’ve now seen a variety of attacks using Artex since then. And since this stuff is open source and the models are open weight, anybody can take these things off the shelf. So I think that was really interesting. And then the other one is the attacks against Fireworks and Railway. These look like they were pulled off by Chinese actors who are interested in the American AI ecosystem. So China has what’s called the cottage-access industry. So effectively there’s an ecosystem of private contractors who will break into Western companies on behalf of the greater Chinese economic ecosystem, with permission of the Chinese government, and somewhat de-duplicated and given cover by the Chinese government for Chinese economic purposes. And the fact that these folks are not going after inference, they’re not going after customer data, they’re going after API keys is really interesting. Because that looks like they’re specifically going after model weights, as well as the data used to train AI. Warzel: Break those last things down for me, just because there’s some terms I think the audience may not be totally familiar with. Stamos: Yeah. So Fireworks is a prominent company that provides training services to companies that want to build their own AI models. And so they were attacked, and the side of Fireworks that was attacked was the side that does training. And so it looks like who attacked them was groups who were helping out Chinese companies. And they were trying to steal information that would then help Chinese AI companies improve their AI models. So there’s now an entire ecosystem of hackers who are working on behalf of Chinese AI companies trying to improve and take data that will help them accelerate their work. Warzel: I want to talk a little bit about the pace of innovation here. Because it seems like the moment we’re heading toward is—the good guys are deploying helpful, protective AI. We’re rewriting the code using the AI to protect against the people who are, you know, using AI agents and systems to attack. How worried does that make you? Given the advancements of these agents, the fact that we’re seeing them, you know, behaving either unexpectedly or communicating in these advanced ways? There was the news recently that OpenAI is no longer conducting frontier-model training with internet access, ’cause the models have been able, you know, to communicate, share information without the internet. Again, it feels like this is all moving really fast, from the innovation standpoint, of understanding what these things can do. How much control, you know, humans have in these systems. And yet they’re also, you know, going to be deployed in this fight on both sides. Like, how much are you worried about the speed with which this is all moving? Stamos: This is the crazy challenge, because we want to have really capable models to help us do cyber defense. In creating these highly capable models, we wanna do so in a way that doesn’t cause damage. You know, OpenAI released, I think, a very good blog post in the work they’re doing to create secure evaluation frameworks. So that’s where I think you’re referring to. What they did was, they asked their best cyber models to then red-team their protections, and it found a bunch of ways. They found ways to sneak information between their different isolation mechanisms. They did timing attacks, they’re called. And stuff like that. Which is, you know, the right thing for them to do. And I’m glad that they documented this, ’cause it helps the rest of us who do model training. At Cognition, we do model training, so it was very helpful for them to document this. And we’re working with them and Anthropic to try to align how we all do this work. It’s really important to continue to push the frontier forward. I think there’s honestly been—it’s great to talk about Hugging Face and stuff. Models escaping from frontier labs is not the long-term risk, to be frank. The long-term problem is models being misused by humans to do bad things. I think I am not a P(doomer) of thinking the models themselves are going to have their own desire to do bad things. Warzel: Sure. It’s a human problem, yeah. Stamos: Yeah; I think there are reasons. You know, I think the labs are coordinating on like reasonable limits of what we do in training. Of making sure that these things don’t encrypt their chain of thought; making sure that there are reasonable limits put on them. I am much more worried about the capabilities that are released. And then, to that extent, I think what we need to really align on is how—and I think this is actually quite difficult. We have to provide cyber capabilities for defense. How do you do that without allowing those cyber capabilities to be used for offense in a negative way? And that’s spectacularly hard. And the other problem here is that governments, especially the United States government, have not defined what kind of liability companies have when they do this. And so in the defensive cyberworld, we complain a lot about the restrictions put on the frontier models here. Warzel: But let me push just a little bit. That all makes complete sense. But it feels to me, and I think it feels to people who are just on the outside of all of this looking in, that this doesn’t feel like a sustainable moment. Or the things that, you know—the speed with which this is all happening is very concerning. It makes the challenge harder and harder. Like, help me understand the logic of “we have to push this forward.” Also we’re starting to see things accelerate in a way that is genuinely concerning, that, you know—South Korean banks are now on the table here. It feels like there is a disconnect in that logic, I think, to lots of people. So I’d love for you to just, you know, explain why we should continue to move forward with this, given those fears. Stamos: Look, I work on cyber defense. And one, these bugs already exist; these vulnerabilities exist. And so I don’t think that there is a good way to just kind of pause the world at this point, because the capabilities that exist at this point are enough to find a huge number of flaws. So a tiny portion of the code that’s ever been written has now been scanned by the high-end cyber models, and bugs found and/or exploited. A tiny portion, right? Part of the problem here is the coordination problem. If I could pause everybody, to try to figure out a safety regime here, I would. But I don’t have that power. And so personally, what I would like to do is, I would like to focus on finding these bugs and fixing them. I would like to focus on building better defensive capabilities. And then especially on the cost issue, because the cost of the high-end defensive capabilities is way too high. You can’t afford to run Mythos against all of this code and fix it. So we have to focus on lowering the cost and fix—of both finding the bugs and especially fixing them. And so that’s something we’re really focused on at Cognition—is like the Pareto frontier between cyber capability and cost. So you’re right that is the issue. I agree. I don’t have power—sorry, Charlie—to fix that. And from my perspective, what I’m personally working on is just trying to then deal with the reality of—the frontier is moving incredibly quickly. And how do we deal with that fact? And what we do is, we try to fix those things as fast as possible and then build the defensive models as quickly as possible. Warzel: Are we maybe also seeing some resiliency of the systems? You know, when you think about the PHP bug—the big splashy one from the last couple weeks—it hasn’t really produced any big mass compromises, right? Like, I haven’t seen the follow-up story of, you know, People are in, and all this information got stolen . The response to it seemed pretty orderly, pretty well coordinated. Is that the system working? Or is that just kind of an aberration and a quiet before the storm? Stamos: We got very lucky. The PHP bug turns out to be quite hard to exploit. Also a lot of those 70 percent of sites are behind Cloudflare or another CDN, and those guys put in protections because of the coordinated-disclosure process. So I think we got lucky with the PHP bug that while it, in theory, is exploitable, in practice it was much less exploitable than it looked in the first case. So it looks like it was kind of a near-miss; the asteroid that grazed the atmosphere and gave us a good warning. Yeah, so we got lucky on this one. But what you saw with the Hugging Face bug was OpenAI’s agent swarm found bugs in Hugging Face that were specific to Hugging Face, wrote the exploits—and then just threw them away, and then found new ones. Because these things are so fast that they can do that. And so that’s much more what I’m worried about than the off-the-shelf bugs—is the AI agents finding custom stuff for each web app, for each API. Warzel: So given everything that we’ve talked about, I wanna end here by—again, the people who are consuming this news from afar, I think, are a little overwhelmed by it. In some cases, if they’re not a cybersecurity professional, there’s not a ton that you can do to help out in this ecosystem. But what should people be doing right now, in this moment on a personal level, to shore up? Make sure they’re as ready and prepared as possible for this more, you know, insecure version of the internet? Stamos: Yeah. So honestly, it’s the same stuff you should have been doing five years ago. But now it’s just more important, right? So the first thing is, the No. 1 way any normal person gets hacked is by reusing the same password everywhere. I know you would never do this, Charlie, or anybody who’s watching this podcast, but a lot of people use the same password in lots of places. You don’t do that, because what happens is some bad website gets hacked, and then the password gets stolen, and then that happens to be password you use for your Gmail or your bank. And especially, if your email gets taken over, your life’s over, because all of your passwords get taken. So use a password manager, something like 1Password, and go reset all of your passwords. Make sure they’re all different. And then have one really good password for your password manager, and keep that in your head. Or even write it down on a piece of paper. A password on a Post-it note in your wallet or your purse can’t be stolen from thousands of miles away. So change all your passwords; have them all be different. Use passkeys if possible, right? So having passkeys in the password manager, or on your phone, is really key. The second is just—people are just gonna have to be more paranoid. Both because of all the theft of personal information that’s gonna happen, as well as the rise of AI voice, AI, the creation of video. We’re gonna see a real rise in scams that are very realistic. So people are getting phone calls that sound like their grandchild has been kidnapped. People are getting more spam text messages. If it seems too good to be true, if it seems like something is fake, it probably is. And so people just need to be more paranoid. Go help your parents and your grandparents be more paranoid. The third thing is—if you can use a limited computer, do it, right? Warzel: So what is a limited computer? Stamos: I bought my parents and my in-laws Chromebooks for Thanksgiving one year, and it made my holiday so much better, right? So if you just use a web browser all the time, then you do not need a full Windows computer or Mac. If you’re just in Chrome all day, or Safari, then you can get a Chromebook, or you can get an iPad, and you can live in that. Those are much more secure than like a full computer that can run malware. And so get a Chromebook, or get an iPad, especially for the slightly older people in your life. That’s a much safer option. And I think what’s going to happen, because things are just gonna get a little less trustworthy, it’s possible that people are just gonna have secondary sock-puppet accounts. So like, have a secondary identity for the stuff in your life that you don’t really care about, right? So have that second Gmail account that’s not charliew@gmail. You can have the surferboy1985@gmail, and use that for all the things—for, you know, your betting site and the other things that you don’t care about. It’s not a bad idea to have kind of a secondary identity, so that if it’s compromised, it doesn’t lead back to your bank. It doesn’t lead back to the things you care about. Warzel: Thank you. We’re entering a brave new world, and I genuinely appreciate the advice on all this and helping to contextualize it. Alex Stamos, thanks for coming on Galaxy Brain . Stamos: Yeah; thanks for covering it, Charlie. Great to see you. Warzel: That’s it for us here. Thank you again to my guest, Alex Stamos. If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, or on Apple, or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you’d like to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. And just a reminder: We’re still prepping for a Galaxy Brain AMA episode. You can send all inquiries about the show, about my work, about AI, about cybersecurity, and how safe your bank account is. Pretty much anything. Send me an email at charlie@theatlantic.com, subject line: “Galaxy Brain AMA.” Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

items.title: Journalisme en Afrique : précarité, menaces et autocensure
items.description: © Internet Précarité salariale, absence de protection sociale, menaces et autocensure pèsent sur l’exercice du journalisme en Afrique. Un rapport de la Fédération des journalistes africains (FAJ), présenté le 25 octobre à Addis-Abeba, dresse un état des lieux à partir d’une enquête menée auprès de 1 586 professionnels dans 45 pays. Exercer le métier de journaliste reste difficile pour une large partie des professionnels interrogés. Aux risques liés à la collecte et au traitement de l’information s’ajoutent une précarité économique persistante et des pressions qui peuvent fragiliser leur indépendance. Selon le rapport, 61 % des répondants affirment que leurs revenus tirés du journalisme ne leur permettent pas de couvrir leurs besoins essentiels. Intitulé Le journalisme assiégé : conditions de travail épouvantables et déclin de la liberté de la presse en Afrique, le document rassemble les réponses de journalistes des cinq régions du continent. Quelque 58 % déclarent subir des retards de salaire, 62 % travaillent sans contrat écrit et 71 % ne bénéficient d’aucune protection sociale. Seuls 4 % estiment que leur rémunération couvre convenablement leurs dépenses essentielles. Les jeunes sont fortement représentés dans l’enquête, les 18-34 ans constituant 53 % des répondants. Les pigistes représentent 29 % de l’échantillon et les collaborateurs et correspondants 18 %. La peur au quotidien À cette fragilité économique s’ajoute l’insécurité. Quelque 65 % des journalistes interrogés déclarent avoir subi des menaces ou des actes d’intimidation liés à leur travail au cours des trois dernières années. Seuls 17 % disent se sentir toujours en sécurité dans l’exercice de leur profession, tandis que 55 % éprouvent rarement ou jamais ce sentiment. Le bilan humain rappelle les risques du métier. Selon la Fédération internationale des journalistes, 18 journalistes et professionnels des médias ont perdu la vie en Afrique en 2025, dont plusieurs dans des circonstances accidentelles liées à leur activité. Les pressions influencent aussi directement le traitement de l’information. Quelque 84 % des répondants reconnaissent pratiquer l’autocensure, occasionnellement ou fréquemment, et 69 % ont déjà évité certains sujets par crainte de menaces. L’ingérence politique est considérée comme la principale menace contre la liberté de la presse par 29 % des personnes interrogées, devant les violences contre les journalistes, citées par 22 %, et les lois restrictives, par 18 %. Parmi les violations effectivement subies figurent les ingérences politiques pour 68 %, les obstacles à l’accès à l’information pour 61 %, la censure pour 57 % et l’intimidation judiciaire pour 49 %. Au total, 65 % jugent la liberté de la presse restreinte ou fortement restreinte dans leur pays. Seuls 6 % la considèrent comme très libre. Les femmes davantage exposées Le rapport insiste également sur les risques numériques. Le harcèlement en ligne concerne 36 % des journalistes interrogés, 26 % déclarent avoir subi une surveillance numérique, 24 % des abus sexuels en ligne et 21 % des tentatives de piratage. Pourtant, 63 % n’ont reçu aucune formation en sécurité numérique. Les femmes journalistes apparaissent particulièrement exposées. Pour 76 % des répondants, elles sont confrontées à des risques supplémentaires, notamment le harcèlement sexuel, les violences en ligne fondées sur le genre, les inégalités salariales et les discriminations professionnelles. La pression affecte aussi le bien-être des journalistes. L’insécurité financière constitue la première source de stress pour 38 % d’entre eux, suivie de la peur des agressions avec 24 %. Par ailleurs, 72 % travaillent dans des structures dépourvues de dispositif de soutien psychologique. Près de 44 % déclarent connaître fréquemment un épuisement professionnel et 47 % ont déjà envisagé de quitter le métier. Face à ces résultats, le président de la FAJ, Omar Faruk Osman, appelle les gouvernements, les employeurs et les institutions concernées à agir sur les conditions de travail. La Fédération réclame notamment des salaires équitables, des contrats écrits, une meilleure protection sociale et des lieux de travail plus sûrs. Elle demande également des enquêtes rapides sur les agressions contre les journalistes, la réforme des législations utilisées pour les intimider, le respect de l’indépendance éditoriale et des mécanismes spécifiques de protection des femmes journalistes. Réalisée avec le soutien du Programme multidonateurs de l’UNESCO sur la liberté d’expression et la sécurité des journalistes, l’enquête relie ainsi les conditions matérielles d’exercice du métier à la liberté d’informer. Salaires insuffisants, absence de contrats, menaces et autocensure affectent à la fois les journalistes et les informations auxquelles le public peut avoir accès. Joseph Amara Dembélé

items.title: SIAO 2026 : les artisans maliens à la conquête de nouveaux marchés à Ouagadougou
items.description: La 18e edition du Salon international de l'artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO) a ouvert ses portes ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026 au Burkina Faso. Pendant dix jours, des artisans venus d'une trentaine de pays exposeront leurs creations et rechercheront de nouvelles opportunites commerciales. Le Mali prend part a ce rendez-vous avec une centaine d'artisans, qui entendent faire connaître leurs produits et nouer des partenariats. Pres de 800 stands accueillent plus de 6 000 exposants venus de 30 pays. Les organisateurs attendent plus de 800 000 visiteurs, dont une centaine d'acheteurs professionnels, pour cette edition du SIAO. Comme lors des precedentes editions, le Mali est fortement represente. Une centaine d'artisans maliens participent a l'evenement, aux cotes d'une delegation du ministere de l'Artisanat, de la Culture, de l'Industrie hoteliere et du Tourisme. « Valorisation des produits locaux » Placee sous le theme « Artisanat africain et industrialisation : quelle synergie pour une meilleure organisation et valorisation des produits locaux et du patrimoine culturel », cette 18e edition met en avant les perspectives de developpement du secteur artisanal africain. Le Ghana est le pays invite d'honneur. La ceremonie officielle d'ouverture a ete presidee par le capitaine Ibrahim Traore, president du Burkina Faso. Un important dispositif securitaire a ete deploye sur le site de la manifestation. L'artisanat malien au-dela des frontieres Pour les artisans maliens, le SIAO represente une occasion de developper leur clientele au-dela des frontieres nationales. C'est notamment l'ambition de Mahamadou Dianka, jeune artisan venu de Bamako, qui participe pour la premiere fois a ce salon. Il y presente des chaussures en cuir pour hommes, femmes et enfants, ainsi que des sacs et des porte-monnaie. Il espere attirer de nombreux clients et nouer des contacts commerciaux. « On attend seulement les clients, beaucoup de clients meme », confie-t-il. Le jeune exposant se dit egalement satisfait de l'organisation du salon. Malgre une arrivee recente et la fatigue du voyage, il a ete agreablement surpris par les conditions d'accueil. « Moi, j'ai participe a beaucoup de foires, mais celle-la m'a meme surpris. L'organisation, meme pour rentrer la, la facon dont j'ai vu, tout est bien », souligne-t-il. Pour cette premiere experience au SIAO, Mahamadou Dianka espere ainsi transformer cette vitrine internationale en opportunites concretes pour ses creations. Ecouter aussi : Le Club Tamani au cœur du SIAMA 5 L’article SIAO 2026 : les artisans maliens à la conquête de nouveaux marchés à Ouagadougou est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Ogra notifies 15.3pc increase in RLNG price for October
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) on Friday notified an increase of up to 15.3 per cent in the price of Regasified Liquefied Natural Gas (RLNG) for sales at the distribution stage by the two Sui gas companies for October, mainly due to higher crude prices. The increase has come after a 20pc price reduction for September. This is expected to have a significant impact on fuel cost for power generation in December. The RLNG-based power generation cost in September amounted to Rs40 per unit based on the average RLNG import price of $10.06 per million British thermal unit (mmBtu), compared to $10.75 per mmBtu in October. The average delivered price ex-ship of LNG for two cargoes in October amounted to $10.75 per mmBtu, compared to $10.06 per mmBtu in September, $12.12 per mmBtu in August and $18.96 per mmBtu in July. Karachi-based Sui Southern Gas Company Limited (SSGCL) serves consumers in Sindh and Balochistan, and its system losses at the distribution stage stand at 12.55 per cent, compared to about 10.6pc last year. On the other hand, Lahore-based Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Limited (SNGPL) provides gas to consumers in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and its system losses at the distribution stage were also reported at almost 9pc against 7.47pc in October last year. According to the notification, RLNG’s sale price for SNGPL at the transmission stage increased by 13.9pc to $15.94 per mmBtu for October compared to $13.99 per mmBtu in September. The sale price at the distribution stage for SNGPL was, thus, increased by 14pc to $17.33 per mmBtu for October, against $15.196 per mmBtu in September. Meanwhile, RLNG sale price for SSGCL has been increased at the transmission stage by 15.25pc to $14.53 per mmBtu for October, against $12.611 per mmBtu in September. The sale price at the distribution stage for the company thus also increased by 15.27pc to $16.396 per mmBtu for October compared to $14.22 in September. Ironically, the inherent cost additions in the supply chain — all of them in the public sector — continue to make the end-RLNG price higher. This can be seen from the fact that the RLNG distribution prices — $16.396 per mmBtu for SSGCL and $17.33 per mmBtu for SNGPL — are almost $6.58 and $5.65 per mmBtu higher than the average $10.75 per mmBtu delivered price ex-ship (DES), respectively. This is mainly because of the fact that both the LNG importers — Pakistan State Oil and Pakistan LNG Limited — and port authorities also charge profit margins on account of retainage and margins, at the rate of 3.77pc of DES price. This is on top of 8.97pc system losses (SNGPL) and 12.55pc losses (SSGCL). The basket RLNG price was based on two cargoes each in October — both from Qatar — under two separate long-term contracts of 13.37pc and 10.20pc of Brent. PSO has a long-term contract for up to 11 cargoes per month, but part of these supplies were usually diverted to the spot market, even before the Middle East crisis , when Qatar declared force majeure after the US attack on Iran, the closing of the Strait of Hormuz and the suspension of gas operations at the field.

items.title: The Currency of the Journal Article Is Collapsing
items.description: Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included bad writing, a lack of relevant citations, and little engagement with previous scholarship, such as a paper that promised a “novel” conceptual framework without acknowledging the many other papers making similar claims. As an associate editor of a bioethics journal, I’d make a quick “desk reject” decision and not send these articles for peer review, which effectively killed any hope of publication. Now I can say: AI is affecting every part of academic publishing. Readers have started to notice that AI-assisted articles are slipping into journals. But AI is creating problems behind the scenes as well. Weak articles now arrive on my desk with fluent prose, plausible-sounding arguments, neatly organized sections, and citations that pass initial AI checks. Only with a deeper look does the AI use become apparent. There are sentences that have all of the trappings of real arguments, but that rarely make sense—like, say, “Algorithmic triage functions less as a clinical tool than as an infrastructure of deferred accountability.” There are citations that refer only to open-access or highly cited articles , because the most popular LLMs can’t readily access paywalled journal articles, so they rely on what’s either free or described at length elsewhere. Unfortunately, the scholars submitting papers aren’t the only ones using AI. So are many of their peer reviewers. One recent peer review that my journal received—from a senior scholar—read like an unedited cut-and-paste job from an LLM. The giveaway was that it criticized the authors for failing to cite a particular text—in this case, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders —when the paper did indeed cite it. [ Read: The rise of parasite authors ] Some of my own papers have received similarly suspicious peer reviews. A recent one of a paper that I had co-authored came in the telltale header-bullet style of ChatGPT, requesting 22 major and 14 minor edits on matters spanning ethics, statistics, experimental design, and machine learning. A review by a human typically comes from somewhere; I can usually tell, without knowing the name, whether a reviewer is a philosopher or a social scientist. But this review came from both everywhere and nowhere. The prose sparkled (human reviewers don’t take the time to polish text that no one but the authors and editors will see); the review quibbled with an inessential word and offered three synonyms to use instead (reviewers will object to a word or phrase, but they don’t usually supply a thesaurus-like menu of alternatives); and it questioned the year a reference was published (reviewers regularly check sources, but not the accuracy of small bibliographic details). But as every academic knows, peer review has always been a highly imperfect process. One might imagine experts with deep knowledge of a paper’s topic or methods carefully reviewing each manuscript prior to publication. The reality is that those with relevant expertise are overwhelmed with review requests and almost never have the time to write one, particularly if the request comes from a lesser-known journal. (I learned this in my first years as a journal editor, when my review requests to top scholars were mostly ignored or declined.) Although many reviews are thoughtful, others come from people with tangential expertise. (Entire corners of the internet are dedicated to memes from “Reviewer 2,” a caricature of a pedantic scholar who has clearly misunderstood the paper.) When retractions or fabrications make the news , such as the 2024 Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology article that included an AI-generated image of a rat with oversize genitals, the public often reacts with outrage at the failure of the peer-review process. But as a journal editor, I’m surprised it doesn’t happen more often. AI has pushed this already flawed system of peer review to its breaking point. Journals are being inundated with manuscript submissions. Some journals have reported their submissions doubling or even tripling since ChatGPT was released, a few years ago. Across the Elsevier portfolio of journals, submissions were about twice as high in 2025 than in 2024. One journal reported having to double its editors—all unpaid volunteers—to handle the boom in submissions. Reviewing a growing number of submissions with a critical eye now takes time that minimally compensated or unpaid journal editors, including me, do not have. As a result, even as journal editors desk-reject more manuscripts, they are also sending more and more AI-assisted papers out for review, which in turn off-loads the work of picking apart AI-assisted articles to two or three other overworked scholars. These scholars are, in turn, receiving more and more review requests. In some cases, the cycle has become absurd: AI-assisted papers land with overworked editors, who send them to rushed reviewers, who in some cases use AI to write the review, which the authors revise and resubmit using AI. A recent study of 7.3 million journal articles published from 2020 to 2025 found that by 2025, more than half showed evidence of LLM assistance, up from 12 percent in 2023. These problems are most likely to afflict the humanities and social sciences, because conceptual argumentation is easier to mimic than experimental results. But AI can generate much of an article even in the hard sciences. [ Steven Strogatz: A mathematician reads the AI future ] The journal article has long been the currency of academic social capital. Most early-career academics can tell you offhand how many they have published, like a salesperson rattling off their most recent quarter’s numbers. This currency has remained valuable because, until recently, a good article was difficult to produce. Such scholarship required time, sometimes funding, and the expertise to design a study or work through an argument. Currencies collapse when people can no longer trust them. Even if a handful of top-tier journals can preserve the value of their articles, they cannot survive in an academic economy in which tens of thousands of other outlets cannot distinguish serious scholarship from work that just looks like it. Each week, I meet with my trainees to read and critique a journal article in our field. I recently assigned an article with a promising title that had been published in an established journal weeks earlier, which had looked fine after a skimmed read. But as we dissected it, we began to see all of the hallmarks of AI: the sheen without the substance, the citations that were slightly off, the odd absence of conceptual coherence. I’d been on a conference panel with one of the authors earlier that year. Ironically, the topic was the challenges of AI in academic publishing. I can usually find a teachable moment in any situation. But if I can no longer tell my trainees—postdocs and graduate students—that rigorous scholarship has a value that an academic journal can recognize, then I’m not sure what kind of future, exactly, I am preparing them for.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : à la veille d’un moment historique pour l’Afrique, Dakar donne la parole à sa jeunesse
items.description: Permettre aux jeunes d’être en bonne santé, de faire entendre leur voix et de participer aux décisions qui façonnent leur avenir, c’est l’une des ambitions phares de la 3ᵉ édition de la Journée de mobilisation et de plaidoyer (JoMP) 2026. Elle a été tenue vendredi à Dakar à quelques heures de la cérémonie d’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse Dakar 2026 (JOJ Dakar 2026). À quelques heures de l’ouverture des premiers Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse, organisés sur le continent africain, le Prof. Mohamed Janabi, directeur régional de l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS) a participé à la 3ᵉ édition de la Journée de mobilisation et de plaidoyer (JoMP) 2026, consacrée à la santé des jeunes d’Afrique de l’Ouest et du Centre. A lire aussi : JOJ Dakar 2026 : près de 7 000 membres des délégations déjà à Dakar Pour l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS), les JOJ2026 célébreront le talent, l’énergie et la détermination des jeunes. La Journée de mobilisation et de plaidoyer (JoMP) porte une autre dimension essentielle de cette même ambition : leur permettre d’être en bonne santé, de faire entendre leur voix et de participer aux décisions qui façonnent leur avenir. « La santé ne doit pas être une politique abstraite pour nos jeunes. Elle doit être une réalité vécue chaque jour dans les soins auxquels ils ont accès, les espaces où ils évoluent et les possibilités qui leur sont offertes de rester actifs et de s’épanouir », affirme le Professeur Janabi. Faire de Dakar2026 un héritage durable, estime le directeur régional de l’OMS, c’est aussi faire en sorte que chaque jeune puisse grandir en bonne santé et rester actif et devenir acteur des transformations qui le concernent. M. DIEME

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : près de 7 000 membres des délégations déjà à Dakar
items.description: À ce jour, entre 49 % et 50 % des arrivées attendues ont été enregistrées au Sénégal, représentant près de 7 000 membres des délégations des Jeux olympiques de la Jeunesse Dakar 2026. C’est ce qu’a indiqué vendredi, le ministre des Transports terrestres et aériens, Abdoul Ahad Ndiaye. Il s’exprimait lors d’une réunion de la Task Force Mobilité JOJ. Ce vendredi 30 octobre, la Task Force Mobilité JOJ s’est réunie au Transport Operations Center (TROC), pour une séance matinale de coordination et de débriefing consacrée au suivi du dispositif de transport mis en place pour les Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse Dakar 2026. « À la veille de la cérémonie d’ouverture, alors que certaines compétitions démarrent déjà, nos équipes sont pleinement mobilisées pour assurer la fluidité des déplacements des délégations, des participants et du public. À ce jour, entre 49 % et 50 % des arrivées attendues ont été enregistrées au Sénégal, représentant près de 7 000 membres des délégations », a soutenu le ministre Abdoul Ahad Ndiaye. A lire aussi : JOJ Dakar 2026 : un centre de contrôle installé pour une vision consolidée du trafic routier Afin de faciliter les déplacements et l'accès à la cérémonie d'ouverture au stade Abdoulaye Wade de Diamniadio, plusieurs mesures importantes sont mises en place. Il y a 19 000 cartes d’accès gratuits au TER sont prévues pour les personnes accréditées aux Jeux ; la gratuité du TER est également accordée à tous les détenteurs d’un billet pour la cérémonie d’ouverture, afin de faciliter leur accès au stade. « Le service du TER sera exceptionnellement prolongé jusqu’à 3h00 du matin, dans la nuit du samedi 31 octobre au dimanche 01 novembre. Au-delà de la cérémonie d’ouverture, je tiens à souligner que la Task Force Mobilité JOJ, restera pleinement mobilisée tout au long des Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse », a ajouté le ministre. Des réunions régulières de coordination, de suivi et de débriefing permettront, selon lui, d'anticiper les besoins, de traiter les incidences de la journée précédente et d'adapter en permanence le dispositif aux exigences des compétitions. Mariama DIEME
